statement: Problem decomposition - dividing a complex problem into pieces that can be solved independently - is the most fundamental problem in computer science.
Software design skill is developed more through high-quality practice than through innate talent.
The overall goal of software design is to reduce complexity, which matters more than adhering to any individual principle.
Every design principle has limits and exceptions; taking any design idea to an extreme produces a bad result.
The greatest limitation in writing software is a developer's ability to understand the system being built.
Complexity increases inevitably over a program's life and grows harder to manage as the program and its team get larger.
There are two complementary ways to fight complexity: eliminate it by making code simpler and more obvious, and encapsulate it through modular design.
Software design is a continuous process spanning a system's entire lifecycle, unlike the design of physical artifacts.
The waterfall model rarely works for software because a large system's design cannot be visualized completely enough to understand its implications before building it.
Incremental, agile development works for software because software is malleable enough to absorb significant design changes partway through implementation.
The initial design is almost never the best; developers should continually redesign and spend a fraction of their time on design improvements.
There is no simple recipe that guarantees a great design; high-level concepts serve to compare alternatives and guide exploration of the design space.
Learning to recognize red flags - signs that code is more complicated than it needs to be - is one of the best ways to improve design skill.
When a red flag appears, stop and look for an alternative design that removes it.
These design ideas apply beyond object-oriented classes - to functions in non-OO languages and to modules such as subsystems and network services.
Complexity is anything about a software system's structure that makes it hard to understand and modify.
Complexity is what a developer experiences at a given moment for a given task; it does not necessarily correlate with a system's overall size or feature count.
Overall system complexity equals the sum of each part's complexity weighted by the fraction of developer time spent working in that part.
Isolating complexity in a place that is rarely touched is almost as good as eliminating it.
condition: the affected parts are almost never modified

statement: Complexity is more apparent to readers than to writers; if other developers find your code complex, then it is complex.
Complexity manifests in three ways: change amplification, cognitive load, and unknown unknowns.
Change amplification occurs when a seemingly simple change requires code modifications in many different places.
A goal of good design is to reduce the amount of code affected by each design decision.
Cognitive load is how much a developer must know to complete a task; higher load means more time spent and greater risk of bugs.
An approach that takes more lines of code can be simpler when it reduces cognitive load, so lines of code is a poor proxy for complexity.
Unknown unknowns occur when it is not obvious which code must change, or what a developer must know, to complete a task correctly.
Unknown unknowns are the worst manifestation of complexity, because there is no way to discover what information is missing until bugs appear.
A key goal of good design is for the system to be obvious, the opposite of high cognitive load and unknown unknowns.
Complexity is caused by two things: dependencies and obscurity.
A dependency exists when a piece of code cannot be understood or modified in isolation because it relates to other code.
Dependencies are fundamental and cannot be eliminated; a goal of design is to reduce them and make the remaining ones simple and obvious.
Obscurity occurs when important information is not obvious - for example through generic names, missing units, hidden dependencies, or inconsistency.
A need for extensive documentation is often a red flag that the design is not right; the best way to reduce obscurity is to simplify the design.
Dependencies produce change amplification and cognitive load; obscurity produces unknown unknowns and also adds to cognitive load.
Complexity is incremental: it accumulates from hundreds of small dependencies and obscurities rather than one catastrophic error.
To slow the growth of complexity, adopt a zero-tolerance philosophy toward small added complexities.
Tactical programming - focusing on getting code working as fast as possible - makes it nearly impossible to produce a good system design.
Under tactical programming each task adds small complexities that accumulate rapidly, especially when the whole team works that way.
A tactical tornado produces code quickly but leaves complexity that others must clean up, so they are not the real heroes.
Working code is not enough; the long-term structure of the system is the most important thing.
Most code is written by extending an existing code base, so a developer's most important job is to facilitate future extensions.
A developer's primary goal should be to produce a great design that also works, not merely working code.
Strategic programming requires an investment mindset: invest time to improve the design, which slows you slightly now but speeds you up later.
Design investments are both proactive (trying alternative designs, writing documentation) and reactive (fixing design problems when discovered rather than patching around them).
A large up-front design of the entire system is ineffective (it is the waterfall model); make many small continual investments instead.
Spending roughly 10-20% of total development time on design investment is small enough not to wreck schedules yet large enough to pay off.
Poor code quality slows development by at least 20%.
Once a code base degrades into spaghetti it is nearly impossible to fix, and high development costs persist for the product's life.
The best engineers care deeply about good design, so a wrecked code base makes it harder to recruit them.
For startups, the payoff for good or bad design comes quickly, so a tactical approach may not even speed up the first release.
condition: early-stage startup under release pressure

statement: Facebook's move-fast-and-break-things culture made it successful but left an unstable, hard-to-maintain code base, prompting a later shift to move-fast-with-solid-infrastructure.
Good design must be invested in continually so small problems do not accumulate, and it pays for itself sooner than expected.
Treat design investment as something to do today, not tomorrow; delaying improvements is a slippery slope into a tactical culture.
Modular design lets a developer face only a small fraction of a system's overall complexity at any one time.
A module has two parts - an interface (everything another developer must know to use it) and an implementation.
The goal of modular design is to minimize the dependencies between modules.
A developer should need to understand the interface and implementation of their own module plus only the interfaces of the modules it invokes.
The best modules have interfaces much simpler than their implementations, so changes that do not alter the interface do not affect other modules.
An interface has formal parts (signatures and types, checkable by the language) and informal parts (behavior and usage constraints, describable only in comments).
For most interfaces the informal aspects are larger and more complex than the formal aspects.
An abstraction is a simplified view of an entity that omits unimportant details.
A detail may be omitted from an abstraction only if it is genuinely unimportant; the design goal is to minimize the amount of information that is important.
An abstraction can fail by including unimportant details (adding cognitive load) or by omitting important ones (a false abstraction that creates obscurity).
The best modules are deep: they provide powerful functionality behind a simple interface.
Module depth is a cost-benefit trade-off - benefit is functionality, cost is interface complexity - so more or larger interfaces are not necessarily better.
Unix file I/O, with five simple system calls hiding hundreds of thousands of lines of implementation, is an example of a deep interface.
A garbage collector is a deep module with essentially no interface; adding it shrinks a system's overall interface by removing manual memory freeing.
A shallow module has an interface that is complex relative to the functionality it provides (for example a linked-list class or a one-line pass-through method).
Small modules tend to be shallow.
The conventional wisdom that classes and methods should be small (splitting anything over N lines) produces many shallow units and increases system complexity.
Classitis - the mistaken belief that more classes are always better - yields individually simple classes but greater overall system complexity and verbose boilerplate.
Interfaces should be designed to make the common case as simple as possible.
Because almost every user of file I/O wants buffering, it should be on by default, with any opt-out cleanly separated so most developers never see it.
If an interface has many features but most developers need only a few, its effective complexity is just that of the commonly used features.
Information hiding is the most important technique for achieving deep modules.
Each module should encapsulate its design-decision knowledge in its implementation rather than exposing it in its interface.
Information hiding reduces complexity by simplifying the interface (less cognitive load) and by making the system easier to evolve (no external dependencies on hidden information).
When designing a module, deliberately consider what information can be hidden; hiding more lets you simplify the interface and makes the module deeper.
Declaring variables or methods private is not the same as information hiding, because the information can still leak through public getters and setters.
Total information hiding is best, but partial information hiding - keeping rarely needed information behind separate methods - also has value.
Information leakage occurs when a design decision is reflected in multiple modules, creating a dependency between them.
Information can leak even when it does not appear in any interface (such as two classes that both know a file format), and such back-door leakage is more pernicious because it is not obvious.
Information leakage is one of the most important red flags; develop a high sensitivity to it.
To fix information leakage, merge small closely tied classes or extract the shared knowledge into a new class - but only if a simple abstracting interface exists.
condition: a simple interface that abstracts away the details is available

statement: Temporal decomposition - structuring a system around the time order of operations - is a common cause of information leakage.
When decomposing into modules, organize around the knowledge needed for each task, not the order in which tasks occur.
Information hiding can often be improved by making a class slightly larger, to bring related code together and raise the level of the interface.
Avoid exposing internal data structures (such as returning an internal map), because callers then break whenever the representation changes.
Classes should do the right thing automatically without being asked; sensible defaults (such as an HTTP response version and date) are an example.
Information hiding makes sense only when the hidden information is not needed outside the module; if it is needed outside, it must be exposed.
exception: the information is required outside the module, e.g., performance-affecting configuration

statement: A common design choice is general-purpose vs special-purpose: a general-purpose solution may find unanticipated future uses but risks unused facilities and a poorer fit for today's problem.
The sweet spot is to make a module somewhat general-purpose: its functionality reflects current needs while its interface is general enough to support multiple uses.
condition: do not make it so general it becomes hard to use for current needs

statement: A somewhat general-purpose approach yields simpler and deeper interfaces than a special-purpose one, even when the module is only ever used for its original purpose.
Special-purpose APIs that mirror higher-level features produce many shallow methods and a high cognitive load.
Specializing a lower-level module to a higher-level module's features creates information leakage and ties the two classes together.
A general-purpose API should be defined only in terms of basic features, not the higher-level operations built on top of it.
A false abstraction hides information that the caller actually needs; when details matter, make them explicit and obvious rather than hiding them.
One of the most important elements of software design is determining who needs to know what, and when.
To find the right general/special balance, ask: what is the simplest interface covering all current needs, in how many situations will a method be used, and is the API easy to use for current needs?
Reducing the number of methods in an API is worthwhile only if each method's interface stays simple, not if it requires many extra arguments.
condition: each individual method's API remains simple

statement: A method designed for a single particular use is a red flag that it may be too special-purpose.
Making modules somewhat general-purpose is one of the best ways to reduce overall system complexity.
Software is composed in layers, and in a well-designed system each layer provides a different abstraction from the layers above and below it.
Adjacent layers with similar abstractions are a red flag indicating a problem with the class decomposition.
A pass-through method does little but invoke another method with a similar signature; it makes a class shallower and adds dependencies without adding functionality.
Pass-through methods indicate confusion over the division of responsibility; the interface to a piece of functionality should live in the same class that implements it.
Fix pass-through methods by giving each class a distinct, coherent set of responsibilities - expose the lower class directly, redistribute functionality, or merge the classes.
Multiple methods sharing a signature are acceptable when each contributes distinct functionality, as with a dispatcher or several implementations of one interface.
exception: each method provides useful and distinct functionality

statement: Several methods that implement the same interface reduce cognitive load, because learning one makes the others easier to use.
The decorator pattern encourages API duplication across layers; decorators tend to be shallow, and overusing them produces an explosion of shallow classes.
Before creating a decorator, consider alternatives: add the functionality to the underlying class, merge it with the use case, merge it into an existing decorator, or implement it standalone.
A class's interface should normally differ from its implementation; if the internal representation and the interface share the same abstraction, the class is probably not deep.
A pass-through variable, passed down a long chain of methods, adds complexity by forcing intermediate methods to know about it, and adding a new one means changing many interfaces.
Global variables avoid pass-through variables but create other problems, such as preventing two independent instances of a system in one process (which matters for testing).
A context object holds a system's global state, lets multiple instances coexist in one process, and eases testing; storing a context reference in major objects keeps it out of most signatures.
Each piece of design infrastructure (an interface, argument, class, or definition) adds complexity, so it is justified only if it removes more complexity than it adds.
When you encounter unavoidable complexity related to a module's functionality, handle it inside the module rather than exposing it to users.
condition: the complexity is related to the module's functionality

statement: Most modules have more users than developers, so it is better for the module's developer to suffer the complexity than its users.
It is more important for a module to have a simple interface than a simple implementation.
Throwing an exception or adding configuration parameters to punt a hard decision amplifies complexity, forcing many people to deal with a problem instead of one.
Avoid configuration parameters as much as possible; before adding one, ask whether users can really determine a better value than the code itself can.
When configuration parameters are necessary, compute sensible defaults automatically so users only need to override them under exceptional conditions.
A configuration parameter that could have been computed automatically (such as a retry interval derived from measured round-trip time) yields an incomplete solution that can also become stale.
Pull complexity downward only when it is closely related to the class's existing functionality, doing so simplifies many places elsewhere, and it simplifies the class's interface.
condition: all three conditions hold (related, simplifies elsewhere, simplifies the interface)

statement: When deciding to combine or separate functionality, the goal is to reduce overall system complexity and improve modularity.
Subdivision itself adds complexity: more components to track, more interfaces, extra management code, greater separation, and possible duplication.
If two components are truly independent, separating them is good; if there are dependencies between them, separation is harmful.
condition: the components are truly independent
exception: there are dependencies between the components

statement: Bring code together when it is closely related - indicators include shared information, being used together bidirectionally, conceptual overlap, or being hard to understand one piece without the other.
Bring code together when the pieces share information, so that knowledge of a format or structure lives in one place.
Bring code together when doing so simplifies the interface, for example by eliminating an intermediate interface or enabling automatic behavior like default buffering.
Eliminate duplication by factoring repeated code into a method - most effective when the snippet is long and the replacement method has a simple signature.
condition: the repeated snippet is long and the replacement signature is simple

statement: A general-purpose mechanism should provide only that mechanism and not contain code specializing it for a particular use; special-purpose code belongs in a separate, higher-level module.
Lower layers tend to be general-purpose and upper layers special-purpose, so push special-purpose code upward and keep lower layers general.
The decision to split or join a method should be based on complexity, not on length.
Length alone is rarely a good reason to split a method, and developers tend to break methods up too much.
A long method is not necessarily bad; a long method with a simple signature that is easy to read is deep, which is good.
Each method should do one thing and do it completely.
Split a method only when it yields cleaner abstractions - ideally by factoring out a cleanly separable, general-purpose subtask while leaving the parent's interface unchanged.
condition: the subtask is cleanly separable and the split produces cleaner abstractions

statement: Conjoined methods - where you cannot understand one without understanding the other - are a red flag, as are any two physically separated pieces of code each understandable only via the other.
Joining methods can simplify a system by replacing shallow methods with a deeper one, removing duplication or intermediate data structures, improving encapsulation, or simplifying the interface.
Exception handling is one of the worst sources of complexity, and exception-handling code is inherently harder to write than normal-case code.
The key to taming exceptions is to reduce the number of places where they must be handled, often by redefining an operation's semantics so the normal behavior covers all situations.
Exception-handling code rarely executes in running systems, so it is hard to test and its bugs go undetected - code that has not been executed does not work.
A study of distributed data-intensive systems found that more than 90% of catastrophic failures were caused by incorrect error handling.
condition: distributed data-intensive systems

statement: Programmers worsen exception complexity by defining unnecessary exceptions in an over-defensive style.
The exceptions a class throws are part of its interface, so classes with many exceptions have more complex interfaces and are shallower.
The best way to eliminate exception-handling complexity is to define errors out of existence by designing APIs that have no exceptions to handle.
Redefining an operation's semantics - for example defining unset as ensuring a variable no longer exists - can remove the error case entirely.
Unix file deletion (mark for deletion and defer until the file is closed) defines two classes of error out of existence, unlike the Windows approach that forbids deleting an open file.
Java's substring throwing IndexOutOfBoundsException is unnecessary; an API that automatically clamps the range (like Python's list slices) is simpler, deeper, and more functional.
The best overall way to reduce bugs is to make software simpler.

Exception masking detects and handles a condition at a low level so higher levels need not be aware of it (as TCP resends lost packets and NFS retries), pulling complexity downward and deepening the class.
condition: the exception information is not needed at higher levels

statement: Exception aggregation handles many exceptions with a single handler high in the stack (such as a top-level web dispatcher generating error responses for all missing parameters).
Aggregation works best when an exception propagates several levels up before being handled, whereas masking works best low; both place a handler where it catches the most exceptions.
Error promotion - turning many small errors into one larger recovery path (as RAMCloud crashes a server on object corruption) - reuses a single general-purpose recovery mechanism.
condition: the promoted errors are rare
exception: errors that occur frequently

statement: Crashing the application is a legitimate response to errors that are difficult or impossible to handle and that occur rarely: print diagnostics and abort.
condition: the error is rare and hard or impossible to handle
exception: the application must preserve data, e.g., a replicated storage system

statement: Because C's malloc forces every caller to check for NULL, it is better to wrap it in a checked allocator that aborts with a message when memory is exhausted.
It rarely makes sense to handle out-of-memory errors, because modern memory seldom runs out and recovery offers too little benefit for the complexity it adds.
Crashing is appropriate for errors with no useful recovery, such as an I/O error on an open file, an unopenable socket, or an internal inconsistency that indicates a bug.
Whether crashing on a given error is acceptable depends on the application; a replicated storage system must recover lost data rather than abort.
exception: systems whose value depends on recovering the lost data

statement: Just as errors can be defined out of existence, so can other special cases, which otherwise riddle code with if statements that are hard to follow and bug-prone.
The best way to remove a special case is to design the normal case so it handles the special case automatically, such as a selection that always exists but may be empty.
Defining away or masking exceptions is appropriate only when the exception information is not needed outside the module.
condition: the exception information is not needed outside the module

statement: Masking errors that callers actually need (such as a network module silently swallowing all failures) goes too far; important information must be exposed even at the cost of interface complexity.
exception: callers need the exception information

statement: The general rule is to hide what is unimportant (the more the better) and expose what is important.
Design it twice: consider multiple genuinely different options for each major design decision, because your first idea is unlikely to be the best.
Pick radically different alternatives and consider a second design even one you expect to be bad, to learn from contrasting their weaknesses.
When comparing design alternatives, the most important consideration for an interface is its ease of use for higher-level software.
The best design may combine features of several alternatives, and when none is attractive the identified problems should drive new designs.
The design-it-twice principle applies at many levels - interface, implementation, and overall module decomposition.
Designing it twice adds little time relative to implementation and reliably yields a better design.
Design-it-twice is hard for very smart people accustomed to their first idea being good enough, yet no one designs a large system correctly on the first try.
In-code documentation is crucial: comments aid understanding, enable abstraction by hiding complexity, and - done correctly - the act of writing them improves the design.
A good design loses much of its value if it is poorly documented.
Good-code-is-self-documenting is a myth, because much design information - informal interface behavior, rationale, calling conditions - cannot be expressed in code.
If users must read a method's code in order to use it, then there is no abstraction, because all of the method's complexity is exposed.
The no-time-for-comments excuse fails the investment mindset: writing comments adds on the order of 10% to development time and quickly pays for itself.
Comments do go out of date, but keeping them current is manageable by avoiding duplication, keeping documentation near the code, and using code reviews.
The purpose of comments is to capture information that was in the designer's mind but could not be represented in the code.
Good documentation reduces cognitive load and unknown unknowns and clarifies dependencies and obscurity.
Comments should describe things that are not obvious from the code.
Developers should be able to understand the abstraction a module provides from its declarations and comments alone, without reading its code.
Adopt commenting conventions (following a documentation tool such as Javadoc, Doxygen, or godoc); conventions ensure consistency and make it more likely that comments get written at all.
Every class, every class variable, and every method should have an interface comment.
Do not write comments that merely repeat the code; the test is whether someone could write the comment just by looking at the adjacent code.
Use different words in a comment from those in the name of the entity it documents, adding information about meaning.
Comments add value by describing the code at a different level of detail than the code itself.
Lower-level comments add precision - units, inclusive/exclusive bounds, the meaning of null, ownership of resources, invariants - and are most useful on variable declarations.
When documenting a variable, describe what it represents (think nouns), not how it is manipulated (verbs).
Higher-level comments enhance intuition by describing overall intent and structure; they are harder to write but more valuable.
Comments that explain why code is executed, or under what conditions a method is invoked, are especially helpful.
Separate interface comments from implementation comments so that users of an abstraction are not exposed to implementation details.
If an interface comment must also describe the implementation, the class or method is shallow - so writing comments gives clues about design quality.
A method's interface comment must document its behavior, each argument and return value, side effects, exceptions, and any preconditions, and preconditions should be minimized.
Implementation comments should explain what the code does and why, not how, with a comment before each major block or complex loop.
Document the reasoning behind tricky or non-obvious code (such as a bug fix), referencing the bug tracker rather than duplicating its details.

Cross-module design decisions are complex, cause many bugs, and need documentation placed where developers will discover it - for example a central designNotes file with short pointers from the affected code.
Whether something is obvious is judged from the perspective of a first-time reader, not the author; if a reviewer says it is not obvious, then it is not obvious.
Choosing names is an underrated part of design: good names act as documentation, reduce other documentation, and help detect errors, while poor names create complexity and bugs.
Naming illustrates that complexity is incremental: one mediocre name barely matters, but a system has thousands of names, so good naming has a significant cumulative effect.
A single poorly chosen name can cause a severe bug, as when one variable name was used for both physical and logical block numbers in the Sprite operating system.
Do not settle for names that are merely reasonably close; take extra time to choose names that are precise, unambiguous, and intuitive.
A name should create an accurate image in the reader's mind of what the entity is and is not, using only a few words.
Names are a form of abstraction: the best names emphasize what is most important about an entity and omit less important details.
Good names have two essential properties: precision and consistency.
The most common naming problem is names that are too generic or vague, so readers cannot tell what they refer to.
Boolean variable names should be predicates that make clear what true and false mean.
Precise naming has exceptions: short generic loop variables like i and j are fine when the loop spans only a few lines, and a name can also be too specific.
exception: the variable's entire scope of use is visible within a few lines

statement: Difficulty finding a precise, intuitive, short name for something is a red flag that the underlying entity may lack a clear definition or clean design.
Use names consistently: always use the agreed name for its purpose, never use it for anything else, and keep that purpose narrow enough that every instance behaves the same.
For multiple variables of the same kind, use the common name with a distinguishing prefix (such as srcFileBlock and dstFileBlock), and use i for outer and j for nested loops.
Readability is determined by readers, not writers; the greater the distance between a name's declaration and its uses, the longer the name should be.
Write comments first - at the start, as you write the code - so documentation becomes part of the design process, producing better comments and better designs.
Delayed comments are bad comments: postponed documentation often never gets written, and when written late it is rushed, repeats the code, and omits forgotten design rationale.

The comments-first workflow is: class interface comment, then method interface comments and signatures with empty bodies, iterate, then instance-variable comments, then fill in bodies with implementation comments.
Comments serve as a canary for complexity: if a method or variable needs a long comment, that is a red flag of a poor abstraction.
Writing comments early lets you evaluate and fix design decisions before writing implementation code.
Comments are only a good indicator of design complexity when they are complete and clear.
condition: the comments are complete and clear

statement: Writing comments first is not significantly more expensive, since comments are only about 5% of development time and stable up-front abstractions can save coding time.
A software system's design evolves continuously, and a mature system's design is shaped more by changes made during evolution than by the initial conception.
Stay strategic when modifying existing code; the common smallest-possible-change mindset is tactical and steadily degrades the design.
Ideally, after each change the system has the structure it would have had if it had been designed from the start with that change in mind.
Whenever you modify code, try to improve the system design at least a little; if you are not making the design better, you are probably making it worse.
The investment mindset sometimes conflicts with commercial reality, so a quick-and-dirty fix is occasionally necessary under tight deadlines or when refactoring would break many other teams.
exception: a tight deadline or wide-ranging incompatibilities make full refactoring impractical

statement: Resist quick-fix compromises where possible, ask whether it is the cleanest design achievable given constraints, and plan for every organization to spend a fraction of effort on cleanup and refactoring.
Keep comments close to the code they describe so developers see and update them when changing the code; the farther a comment is, the less likely it stays accurate.
Spread implementation comments to the narrowest scope covering the code they describe rather than massing them at the top of a method, while a short top-of-method strategy comment can still help.
The farther a comment is from the code it describes, the more abstract it should be, to reduce the chance that code changes invalidate it.
Documentation belongs in the code, not in the commit log, because developers needing the information are unlikely to scan the repository history for it.
Avoid duplicating documentation: document each design decision exactly once in the most obvious place, with short references from other affected locations.
If information is already documented outside the program (such as a protocol spec or user manual), reference it instead of repeating it in the code.
Do not redocument one module's design decisions inside another module; let readers consult the called method's own interface comments.
Before committing, scan the diff to ensure each change is reflected in the documentation, which also catches leftover debugging code and unfinished TODOs.
Higher-level, more abstract comments are easier to maintain because minor code changes do not invalidate them.
Consistency reduces complexity and makes behavior more obvious by doing similar things in similar ways and dissimilar things differently, creating cognitive leverage.
Consistency reduces mistakes, because inconsistency lets two genuinely different situations look the same and invites false assumptions.
Consistency can be applied at many levels: names, coding style, interfaces, design patterns, and invariants.
Maintain consistency by documenting conventions, enforcing them with automated checkers that block non-conforming commits, and reinforcing them in code reviews.
When working in existing code, follow the conventions you observe there (when in Rome).
Do not change an existing convention merely because you have a better idea; the value of consistency almost always outweighs the value of one approach over another.
condition: change only with significant new information, a clearly superior approach, organizational agreement, and updating all old uses

statement: Consistency taken too far is harmful: forcing dissimilar things into the same approach creates complexity and confusion.
exception: the things being made consistent are actually dissimilar

statement: Obscurity is one of the two main causes of complexity, and the remedy is to write code that is obvious.
Code is obvious when a reader can understand it quickly, with little thought, and their first guesses about its behavior are correct; obvious code needs fewer comments.
Whether code is obvious is judged by readers, so the best way to assess it is through code review; if a reader finds it non-obvious, it is non-obvious.
Techniques that make code obvious include good names, consistency, judicious white space, and compensating comments where non-obviousness is unavoidable.
Things that make code less obvious include event-driven programming, generic containers, mismatched declaration and allocation types, and code that violates reader expectations.
Software should be designed for ease of reading, not ease of writing.
Avoid generic containers such as Pair; define a specific class or structure with meaningful element names and room for documentation.

Make code obvious in three ways: reduce the information a reader needs (abstraction, eliminating special cases), reuse information readers already have (conventions and expectations), and present important information through good names and strategic comments.

Object-oriented mechanisms can support clean design if used carefully, but they do not by themselves guarantee it - shallow classes, complex interfaces, or exposed internal state still create complexity.
Interface inheritance reduces complexity by reusing one interface across multiple implementations, and more implementations make the interface deeper.
Implementation inheritance reduces change amplification but creates dependencies and information leakage between parent and subclasses, so it should be used with caution.
condition: no viable composition-based alternative exists

statement: Before using implementation inheritance, prefer composition (such as helper classes); if it is unavoidable, separate the state managed by the parent from that managed by subclasses.
Agile development's incremental, iterative approach aligns with good design but risks tactical programming by focusing developers on features rather than abstractions.
The increments of software development should be abstractions, not features; once an abstraction is needed, design it cleanly and somewhat general-purpose all at once.
Unit tests facilitate refactoring: a good test suite gives developers the confidence to make structural improvements, whereas without tests they avoid refactoring and complexity accumulates.
Test-driven development focuses attention on getting individual features working rather than on finding the best design, which is tactical programming.
Writing the test first is appropriate when fixing a bug: write a failing test that triggers the bug, then fix it and confirm the test passes.
exception: bug fixing

statement: Design patterns offer clean solutions to common problems, but their greatest risk is over-application; do not force a problem into a pattern when a custom approach is cleaner.
It is better not to expose instance variables at all; getters and setters are shallow methods that violate information hiding and clutter the interface.
Challenge every new development paradigm by asking whether it actually minimizes complexity in large software systems.
Simplicity is the most important idea even for performance, because simpler designs usually run faster.

Neither optimize every statement (which slows development and adds complexity) nor ignore performance (which causes death by a thousand cuts); use basic performance knowledge to choose naturally efficient, clean designs.
Develop an awareness of which operations are fundamentally expensive - network round-trips, disk and flash I/O, dynamic memory allocation, and cache misses.
The best way to learn which operations are expensive is to run micro-benchmarks that measure a single operation in isolation.
When a more efficient approach is just as simple (such as a hash table instead of an ordered map, or inline structures instead of a pointer array), always choose it.
condition: the efficient approach is no more complex than the alternative

statement: When efficiency requires added complexity, it is worthwhile only if the complexity is small and hidden behind the interface; otherwise start simple and optimize later unless there is clear evidence performance will matter.
condition: the added complexity is small and hidden, or there is clear evidence performance will be important

statement: Simpler code tends to run faster: deep classes do more work per call and cause fewer layer crossings, and defined-away special cases need no checks.
Measure before modifying for performance, because programmers' performance intuitions are unreliable even for experts; measurement locates the highest-impact spots and sets a baseline.
After a performance change, re-measure and back out any change that makes no measurable difference, unless it also makes the system simpler.
When there is no fundamental fix, design around the critical path: identify the minimum code that must run in the common case, then build a clean design as close to that ideal as possible.
Remove special cases from the critical path; ideally a single initial test detects all special cases, after which the critical path runs without further special-case checks.
The RAMCloud Buffer rewrite achieved roughly a 2x speedup while shrinking the code about 20%, showing that clean design and high performance are compatible.
Dealing with complexity is the most important challenge in software design, because complexity makes systems hard to build and maintain and often makes them slow.
Good design creates extra work early but pays off quickly through reused modules, durable documentation, and growing skill, and it takes little longer than quick-and-dirty design once mastered.
The difference between a bad programmer and a good programmer is understanding: good programmers understand what they are doing.
Judge all code work by the end result it produces for people; improving code is the means, a good result is the end, and nothing forgives a poor result.
Code quality is the largest problem facing software projects, so most design effort should target improving code quality.
Software problems such as instability and bloat are not inevitable; they arise almost entirely from complexity.
Effective software systems are inherently complex as a whole, so the only workable approach is to keep the individual pieces simple enough to comprehend.
Treat programming as the act of reducing complexity to simplicity.
A good programmer should do everything in their power to make what they write simple for other programmers to use and comprehend.
Simplicity does not mean less code or avoiding advanced technology; sometimes more code or advanced technology produces greater simplicity.
There is no evidence that writing simple code takes longer; over realistic timelines of weeks or months, simple code gets the job done faster than using complexity as a shortcut.
condition: serious development with multi-week or multi-month timelines

statement: Everybody who writes software is a designer; design happens at every level, down to a single line of code.
Do not design by committee; after considering input, each design decision must be made by an individual, not a group.
condition: individuals hold design authority in their own areas
exception: senior or lead developers retain veto over poor decisions

statement: A designer should actively seek feedback and suggestions but make the final decision individually.
The purpose of software is to help people.
Software never exists to help inanimate objects or the computer; even libraries exist to help the programmers who use them.
Use 'how much does this help people?' as the guiding question for software decisions and feature prioritization.
Making money or showing off should not be the purpose of the software itself.
exception: money is a legitimate personal or organizational goal, just not the software's purpose

statement: For each proposed feature, ask how it serves the software's purpose; this resolves implementation uncertainty, builds team agreement, reveals priorities, and identifies removable features.
Software design is a matter of ranking options to choose the best one, not deciding absolute right versus wrong.
The Equation of Software Design: the desirability of a change is directly proportional to its value and inversely proportional to the effort it requires.
Value is the degree to which a change helps anybody anywhere.
Value combines two factors: the probability of value (how likely or often it helps) and the potential value (how much it helps when it does).
A feature with very high potential value but low probability, such as a rarely needed life-saving feature, is still highly valuable.
When calculating a change's value, weigh any harm it may cause against the help it brings.
Features with no users have no immediate value, and a change usually must be released to be valuable; a change that takes too long can end up with zero value.
condition: value depends on reaching users in time

statement: Effort includes every piece of time connected to a change, including research, communication, and thinking, not just programming time.
Effort and value are hard, perhaps impossible, to measure precisely, but an experienced developer can still rank changes by their relative effort and value.
All changes require maintenance over time.
The full Equation of Software Design: desirability is proportional to value now plus future value, divided by effort of implementation plus effort of maintenance.

Because software is maintained for a long time, value-now and effort-of-implementation almost always become insignificant next to long-term future value and maintenance effort, reducing the equation to future value versus maintenance effort.
condition: the system is maintained over a long lifetime
exception: rare cases where present value or implementation effort are large enough to matter

statement: It is more important to reduce the effort of maintenance than the effort of implementation.
Avoid changes whose maintenance effort will eventually outweigh future value; any change whose maintenance grows faster than its value leads to trouble.
Design systems so the effort of maintenance decreases over time toward zero; then the magnitude of future value can never put you in a dangerous position.
Designing for decreasing maintenance often costs more implementation effort, but implementation effort is nearly always insignificant and should mostly be ignored.
Make the quality of your design proportional to the length of future time the system will keep helping people.
condition: longer expected lifespan demands higher design quality

statement: When a system's lifespan is uncertain, design as if it will be used for a long time: keep it flexible, avoid irreversible decisions, and invest in design.
There are things about the future you cannot know; in software design you cannot know most things about the future.
The most common and disastrous error programmers make is predicting something about the future that they cannot actually know.
You are safest making design decisions from immediately known present-time information rather than predicting the future.
exception: limited exceptions exist for a very near, very certain short-term future

statement: Designing to allow for future change is different from predicting the future; accommodate change without predicting its specifics.
Guiding principles, the laws and rules of software design, keep software working well no matter what the future brings.
The Law of Change: the longer a program exists, the more probable it is that any given piece of it will have to change.
Do not try to predict what will change; knowing that things will change, write software as flexible as reasonably possible.

Empirical history of a long-lived program shows files accumulate far more total changes than their original line counts, with change ratios from 1.6x to 36x, so more work goes into changing a file than writing it.
Once a file has existed long enough, you are more likely to have changed a given line than to currently have it, because total changes exceed the current line count.
The three flaws designers commit when coping with change, in order of frequency, are writing code that isn't needed, not making code easy to change, and being too generic.
Don't write code until you actually need it, and remove any code that isn't being used.
Writing code before it is needed wastes time because it must be redesigned for real needs, and unused code suffers bit rot and hidden bugs.
You cannot write a system that never needs to change while it still has users.
Rigid, hard-to-change design comes from making too many assumptions about the future or writing code without enough design.
Design code based on what you know now, not on what you think will happen in the future.
exception: keep possible future requirements in mind without designing for them speculatively

statement: Keep individual changes small, because a small change is easy to do real design on.
Be only as generic as you know you need to be right now.
condition: genericity justified by present known needs

statement: Overengineering is designing or building too much for your situation; when your design makes things more complex instead of simpler, you are overengineering.
Code that is too generic handles specifics poorly, as when code treating all input as bytes can only report 'bad bytes' instead of 'bad picture'.
Use incremental development and design, building and redesigning the system piece by piece simplest-first, to avoid the three flaws by construction.
In incremental development, redesign the existing system to make the next feature easy to add before implementing that feature.
Order incremental work by what is simplest at each step, avoiding large logical jumps between steps.
Good programmers introduce roughly one defect per 100 lines of code; the best, under the best conditions, about one per 1,000 lines.
The Law of Defect Probability: the chance of introducing a defect is proportional to the size of the changes you make.
Smaller changes produce fewer defects and therefore lower maintenance effort.
The Law of Change and the Law of Defect Probability conflict, since software must change but change introduces defects, and resolving that conflict is precisely why design is needed.
The best design is the one that allows for the most change in the environment with the least change in the software.
Never fix anything unless it is a problem and you have evidence that the problem really exists.
Fixing problems without evidence risks breaking things, wastes time, and adds complexity for no reason.
A user report is not automatically a real problem; treat a behavior as a bug when a significant number of users consider it one, not when only one or two do.
condition: judged by a significant number of users, not one or two

statement: A pattern of confused or duplicate feature requests signals that users cannot find existing features, a discoverability problem worth fixing.
Avoid premature optimization: only optimize the specific parts you can show cause a real performance problem; elsewhere prioritize flexibility and simplicity over speed.
condition: a real, demonstrated performance problem

statement: Don't Repeat Yourself: in any system, any piece of information should ideally exist only once.
Apply DRY to code as well as data: reuse, call, or include existing code instead of copying and pasting blocks.
Following DRY reduces defects, because less code is written or changed per the Law of Defect Probability, and improves flexibility, because one change replaces many.
The Law of Simplicity: the ease of maintenance of any piece of software is proportional to the simplicity of its individual pieces.
The Law of Simplicity targets individual pieces, not the whole system, because no human can comprehend a whole average program at once, only its pieces.
Like a steel structure built from many simple interchangeable girders rather than a few huge custom pieces, software made of small self-contained pieces is easier to build, fix, and maintain.
The perceived time savings of building software in large complex chunks is illusory; over the long run simplicity is what is efficient, not complexity.
Apply the Law of Simplicity by making individual components as simple as possible and keeping them that way over time.
Simplifying existing code is the most impactful thing you can do right now to reduce maintenance effort, and it requires no prediction of the future.
It is speculated, from observation of many programmers, that a programmer's potential to write good software is limited mainly by their ability to conceive of helping another person.
Simplicity is relative: what counts as simple depends on the target audience, and what is simple to the author can look complex to a newcomer.
To understand how a newcomer sees your code, read code you've never seen and try to grasp the whole program and how you would modify it.
Provide newcomer-oriented documentation, such as a 'New to This Code?' section, written as if the reader knows nothing about the program.
No documentation is worse than complex documentation; do not expect others to already know how your code works.
Simplicity depends on context: the same structure or text can be simple in one setting and complex in another.
Simplicity is always achievable because every task has a limited target audience and context; account for them when designing.
There is rarely a fundamentally superior tool, only a tool that particular people find simpler for the task at hand.
exception: tools can have real defects, the bad-technology problems, that genuinely make them unsuitable

statement: A tool's perceived simplicity is largely driven by familiarity; long use makes a tool feel simpler to that person than alternatives.
If you really want to succeed, make code and products stupid, dumb simple.
Anything usable by normal people is also usable by experts, so extreme simplicity broadens your possible users.
Code's target audience is other programmers; it should seem very simple to them, using as much advanced technology as needed to achieve that simplicity.

How easily code can be learned, through simple docs, simple design, and tutorials, governs how quickly others use it correctly; hard-to-learn code causes misuse, bugs, and a support burden that falls back on you.
Difficulty understanding code is a matter of knowledge, not intelligence; newcomers simply have not learned your code yet.
Be consistent: if you do something one way in one place, do it that way everywhere.
Inconsistent code is harder for a programmer to read and understand.
Consistency can make programming easier, as when a uniformly named field lets one piece of code handle every object that has it.
Make a program behave consistently internally so that familiarity with one part transfers to other parts.
When full simplicity isn't achievable, at least be consistent, because a consistent scheme can be learned once and then known forever.
condition: when you cannot be totally simple

statement: Code is read more often than it is written, so it is important to make code easy to read.
Readability of code depends primarily on how space is occupied by letters and symbols.
Use spacing that is consistent and informs the reader about structure; both too little and too much spacing harm readability.
Making code readable also makes it easier to fix, because readable code exposes bugs such as a condition that can never be true.
When code is both buggy and hard to read, make it readable first, then locate the bugs.
Names should be long enough to fully communicate what something is or does, without being so long they become hard to read.
Choose name length by usage: a name used once on its own line can be long, while one used frequently in complex expressions should be shorter but still communicative.
Comments should explain why something was done when the reason isn't obvious, not what the code is doing.
If what code does isn't obvious, simplify the code; only add a comment describing what it does when you cannot make it simpler.
condition: what-comments are a last resort after simplification fails

statement: Readability is important and usually the first step toward good design, but readable code can still be too complex, so readability is not the whole of simplicity.
People do not naturally build simple systems; without attention to design a system evolves into a massive, complicated beast.
A growing project without good design eventually drowns in complexity and will fail, regardless of the reasons given for the failure.
Good design work is largely invisible and uncredited, because catastrophic failures are noticeable while incremental good design is not.
Complexity builds on complexity and is not linear: each new feature must be coordinated with all existing features, so the cost of adding a feature rises as the number of features grows.
Excellent design can minimize but never eliminate the rising per-feature cost; some extra cost per feature always remains.
If a project's requirements are too complex to ship a first version, trim features and ship something that works, then improve it over time.
condition: unable to release a first version

statement: Complexity is added not only by features but by expanding the software's purpose, adding programmers, changing things that needn't change, lock-in to bad technologies, misunderstanding, poor or no design, and reinventing the wheel.
Generally do not expand the purpose of your software; stick to its existing purpose and do that one thing well.

Adding programmers adds complexity rather than simplifying, as Brooks's Mythical Man-Month points out; a small group of expert programmers is more likely to succeed than a large group of inexpert ones.

Treat every change as adding complexity, including the risk of bugs plus decision, implementation, validation, tracking, and testing time, and make informed decisions about changes rather than changing on a whim.
A technology is 'bad' if it locks you in, will not be flexible enough for future needs, or lacks the quality needed to build simple software with it.
Fully understand the systems and tools you work with; misunderstanding breeds complexity in a vicious cycle, while deeper understanding enables simpler designs.
With poor or no design each new feature multiplies the code's complexity instead of adding a little; design is the work of planning for change.
Don't reinvent the wheel: avoid any large in-house dependency such as a web server, protocol, or major library unless that is your product.
exception: acceptable only when the thing doesn't exist yet, all existing options are lock-in bad technologies, existing options fundamentally cannot meet your needs, or they are unmaintained and you cannot take over maintenance

statement: Complexity-adding decisions are usually slowly and gradually harmful, so they sound harmless when proposed and seem fine early, then stack up into a never-shipping product.
Keep a system's basic purpose simple to keep the whole system as simple as realistically possible; features serving other purposes add complexity fast.
Keep a program's purpose very close to the user's purpose; mismatched purposes make the user's life difficult.
Do not let marketers or managers whose goals, such as being cute, edgy, popular, or using the latest tech, are not aligned with the program's basic purpose decide what the program does.
It is the software designer's or technical manager's job to keep the program on track and never violate its basic purpose.
Focused single-purpose products, where soap cleans, salt salts, and a light bulb lights, have sustained large corporations for decades, showing complexity isn't required for commercial success.
Evaluate a technology before adopting it using three factors: survival potential, interoperability, and attention to quality.
Survival potential is the likelihood a technology keeps being maintained; gauge it from recent release history, responsiveness to bug reports, and an active community or momentum.
Prefer technologies adopted broadly across many vendors and developers over single-vendor ones, since a single vendor may fail or stop maintaining the technology.

Distinguish validly popular technologies, with broad multi-organization use, standards, and many implementations like C, from those popular only through monopoly or lock-in, which actually have poor survival potential.
Interoperability is how easily you can switch away from a technology; prefer technologies you interact with through a standard so you can move to another standard-following system.
Choosing nonstandard systems, such as databases that don't support standards, locks you in and forces a program rewrite to switch later.
Attention to quality is whether recent releases improve, through refactoring and cleanup, fewer security vulnerabilities from poor programming, and becoming easier to use.
Once all practical factors are equal, personal preference for a technology is a valid tiebreaker.
condition: all other practical considerations are equal

statement: When something gets very complex, there is often a design error far below the level where the complexity appears; back up and fix the underlying design.
Treat 'unsolvable complexity' as a sign of a fundamental design problem: clean up the messy existing code first, and adding the new feature becomes simple.
When things get complex, ask 'What problem are you trying to solve?', step way back, and question every assumption to find the simplest solution.
Solve the problem in the abstract, asking how it should be solved in a perfect world rather than how to solve it with your current code, then rework the code to fit.
An inherently complex problem like spell-checking or chess does not require a complex solution, but it does demand harder work to keep the code simple.
Many difficult design problems can be solved by drawing or writing them out on paper.
To fix an over-complex part, redesign its individual pieces in small steps, each as small as you can safely make without introducing further complexity.
The greatest danger in redesign or rewrite is introducing more complexity than you remove, which is why so many redesigns and rewrites fail.
Reduce complexity by splitting one complex piece into several simple ones, for example extracting tiny pieces from a long file one at a time and improving each.
Continuously work toward a system simpler than the one you have now, without trying to conceive a perfect system, until you reach a manageable level of simplicity.
Do not stop writing features for a long time just to redesign; failing to improve from the user's perspective risks losing your users, per the Law of Change.
condition: redesign must not halt user-facing progress for long

statement: Balance feature work and complexity by redesigning specifically to make a target feature or bug-fix easier, then implementing it, alternating regularly between redesign and feature work.

Bugzilla gained support for multiple databases through incremental redesign, adopting standard DB commands, wrapping nonstandard ones in functions, dropping OldDB-specific features, and simplifying then extending the installer, testing after every change, yielding a better and more maintainable system that later supported four databases.
Sprinkling per-variant if-statements throughout a codebase can roughly double its complexity; centralizing and standardizing instead keeps it maintainable.
When you hit unfixable complexity, such as underlying hardware, hide it behind a wrapper that is simple for other programmers to use and understand.
Rewriting a system from the ground up is essentially an admission of design failure.
Not all systems must eventually be rewritten; it is possible to design a system that never needs to be thrown away, just as a well-built and maintained skyscraper need not fall.

Rewrite only in the rare case where all of these hold at once: an accurate estimate from real redesign experiments shows rewriting is more efficient than redesigning, you have a tremendous amount of time, you are a drastically better designer than the original, you will build the new system in simple user-validated steps, and you can maintain the existing system while building the new one.
condition: all five rewrite conditions hold simultaneously

statement: Never stop maintaining a system that is in use so programmers can rewrite it; systems in use must always be maintained.
There is no certainty a program will run in the future, only that it runs now; environment or machine changes can break it.
The Law of Testing: the degree to which you know how your software behaves is the degree to which you have accurately tested it.
Unless you have actually tried it, you do not know that it works, and no proof substitutes for running the software.
Every test must ask a precise question about intended behavior and expect a specific answer; 'works' means behaves as you intended.
The degree of testing spans how many aspects, how recently, and in how many environments you have tested; more recent and broader testing raises confidence the software still works.
After you change a piece of software you no longer know that piece, or the pieces connected to it, still works, so it must be retested; a big enough change means retesting the whole program.
Tests must be accurate, never reporting working-when-broken or broken-when-working, and you must observe their results for them to be valid.
Apply the Law of Testing in practice by writing automated tests for every piece of code and running them after each change to confirm everything still works.

The six laws of software design are: the purpose of software is to help people, the Equation of Software Design, the Law of Change, the Law of Defect Probability, the Law of Simplicity, and the Law of Testing.

The most important ideas are the purpose of software, the reduced Equation of Software Design, and the Law of Simplicity: reduce maintenance effort over implementation effort, and maintenance effort is proportional to system complexity, which comes from the complexity of individual pieces.
Bad code slows a team down; as a codebase accumulates mess, team productivity declines over months toward near-zero.
Cleanup deferred to later tends never to happen (LeBlanc's law: later equals never), so do not postpone cleaning a mess.
The only way to go fast and meet deadlines is to keep code as clean as possible at all times; making a mess to save time slows you down immediately.
Adding more staff to a messy codebase does not restore productivity, because newcomers do not know the design intent and add further mess.
A from-scratch grand redesign to escape a mess is risky: the rewrite races a continually changing old system and can drag on for years, often ending in another mess.
Programmers share responsibility for code quality and should defend the code against schedule pressure as firmly as managers defend the schedule.
A professional declines to create messes under deadline pressure, the way a surgeon refuses to skip hand-washing even when the patient demands it.
Clean code does one thing well: each function, class, and module should be focused on a single purpose, undistracted by surrounding details.
Clean code reads like well-written prose and never obscures the designer's intent, using crisp abstractions and straightforward control flow.
Clean code can be read and enhanced by a developer other than its author; ease of change, not merely ease of reading, is the real test.
Code without tests is not clean; clean code carries unit and acceptance tests regardless of how readable it otherwise is.
Clean code provides one way rather than many to do a given thing, with a clear minimal API and minimal, explicitly-defined dependencies.
Duplication is a primary enemy of clean code; when the same thing is done repeatedly it signals a missing abstraction that should be named and expressed once.

Beck's rules of simple code, in priority order: it runs all the tests, contains no duplication, expresses every design idea in the system, and minimizes the number of entities (classes, methods, functions).
Build small abstractions early (for example, wrapping how an item is found in a collection) so the implementation can be localized and changed later without disturbing callers.
Bad code tempts further degradation: like broken windows, one neglected mess invites more, so messes should not be left in place.
Clean code shows close attention to detail and reads as if its author genuinely cared about every element.
Code is read far more than it is written (a ratio well over 10:1), so optimize for readability even when it makes writing harder; easier-to-read code is ultimately easier to write.
Follow the Boy Scout Rule: leave the code cleaner than you found it; small continual improvements on each check-in keep the codebase from rotting.
Error handling in clean code should be complete and follow an articulated strategy rather than being abbreviated or glossed over.
These clean-code recommendations are one school of thought, not absolutes; adopt them deliberately and remain open to other well-founded practices.

Use intention-revealing names: a variable, function, or class name should say why it exists, what it does, and how it is used; if a name needs a comment to be understood, it fails to reveal its intent.

Avoid disinformation in names: do not use words whose entrenched meaning differs from intent (e.g. accountList for a non-List), near-identical spellings, or look-alike characters such as lowercase l and uppercase O.

Make meaningful distinctions: if two names differ they must differ in meaning; do not satisfy the compiler with number-series (a1, a2) or noise words like Info, Data, or Variable that add no information.
Use pronounceable names, because programming is a social activity and unpronounceable names cannot be discussed.
Use searchable names: restrict single-letter names and bare numeric constants to short local scopes, and let a name's length correspond to the size of its scope.
Avoid encodings in names (Hungarian notation, m_ member prefixes, an I prefix on interfaces); modern type systems and IDEs make them an unnecessary mental burden that impedes change and reading.
Avoid mental mapping: do not force readers to translate a placeholder name into the concept it stands for; clarity is king, so professionals write names others can understand directly.
Name classes with nouns or noun phrases (never a verb) and avoid vague words like Manager, Processor, Data, or Info in a class name.
Name methods with verbs or verb phrases, and name accessors, mutators, and predicates with get, set, and is per the JavaBean convention.
When constructors are overloaded, prefer named static factory methods that describe their arguments, and consider making the constructors private to enforce their use.
Do not be cute or use slang and culture-dependent jokes in names; choose clarity over entertainment value and say what you mean.

Pick one word per abstract concept and keep a consistent lexicon across the codebase; mixing equivalents like fetch, retrieve, and get for the same operation forces readers to memorize which class uses which.
Do not pun: avoid using one word for two different ideas, such as naming both a concatenation and a put-into-collection operation add when their semantics differ.
Use solution-domain (computer-science, pattern, and algorithm) names where the readers are programmers, and fall back to problem-domain names only when no technical term exists.

Add meaningful context by enclosing names in well-named classes or functions (prefer a class such as Address over prefixing), but add no more context than necessary and prefer shorter clear names over gratuitous prefixes.
Do not fear renaming things for the better; modern refactoring tools make renaming cheap and it pays off in readability.
Functions should be small, and then smaller still; the author presents this as hard-won experience rather than a research-backed result.
Blocks within if, else, and while statements should be one line long, usually a call to a well-named function, and a function's indent level should not exceed one or two.
A function should do one thing: it should contain only the steps that are one level of abstraction below its stated name.

A function is doing more than one thing if you can extract another function from it whose name is not merely a restatement of its code, or if it can be divided into sections such as declarations and initializations.

Keep every statement in a function at the same level of abstraction; mixing high- and low-level concepts makes it impossible to tell essential logic from detail and tends to attract more detail over time.
Apply the Stepdown Rule: order functions so the code reads top-down as a narrative, each function followed by those one level of abstraction below it.
Avoid switch statements and if/else chains because they inherently do N things and tend to violate the Single Responsibility and Open-Closed principles.
exception: Tolerate a switch when it appears only once, is used to create polymorphic objects, and is hidden behind an inheritance relationship (for example inside an abstract factory) so the rest of the system cannot see it.

statement: Use descriptive function names: a long descriptive name beats a short enigmatic one and beats a descriptive comment; try several names, and keep phrasing consistent across related functions so the sequence tells a story.
The ideal number of function arguments is zero, then one, then two; three arguments should be avoided where possible and more than three requires very special justification.
Output arguments are harder to understand than input arguments and should be avoided; if a function must change state, it should change the state of its owning object rather than an argument.
Flag (boolean) arguments are bad practice: they announce that a function does more than one thing, so split such a function into two separately named functions.

A single-argument function should follow an expected form (ask a question about the argument, transform-and-return it, or interpret it as an event); when transforming, return the result rather than mutating an output argument.
A dyadic function costs more reader effort than a monadic one, so reduce arguments where possible by making an argument a member variable or extracting a dedicated class.
When a function appears to need more than two or three arguments, wrap the related arguments into their own named class (for example passing a Point center instead of x and y).
Functions should have no hidden side effects: an unexpected side effect creates temporal coupling and order dependence that callers cannot see from the name.
exception: If a temporal coupling is truly unavoidable, make it explicit in the function's name (e.g. checkPasswordAndInitializeSession).

statement: Follow Command-Query Separation: a function should either change the state of an object (a command) or return information about it (a query), but not both.

Prefer throwing exceptions to returning error codes: error codes promote commands used as predicates, deep nesting, and immediate-handling burden, and a shared error enum becomes a dependency magnet, whereas new exception types can be added without recompiling callers.

Extract the bodies of try and catch blocks into their own functions; error handling is one thing, so if a function uses try it should be the first statement and nothing should follow the catch/finally blocks.
Do not repeat yourself: duplication bloats code, multiplies the cost of every change, and multiplies the chance of an error of omission; duplication may be the root of most software ills.

The single-entry/single-exit rules of structured programming chiefly benefit large functions; with small functions an occasional extra return, break, or continue is harmless and can be more expressive, though goto should still be avoided.
condition: functions are very small

statement: Write functions iteratively: get a clumsy first draft working under a covering suite of unit tests, then refine it by extracting functions, renaming, and removing duplication while keeping the tests passing.

Comments are at best a necessary evil; their proper use is to compensate for a failure to express intent in code, so whenever a comment is needed, first look for a way to express that intent in the code instead.

Comments decay and mislead: the older a comment and the farther it drifts from the code it describes, the more likely it is wrong, because programmers cannot reliably maintain them, and an inaccurate comment is worse than none.
The code is the only fully reliable source of truth about what a program does, so expend real effort to minimize comments.
Comments do not make up for bad code: when code is confusing, clean the code rather than write a comment to explain the mess.
Explain yourself in code: prefer extracting a well-named function or variable (e.g. employee.isEligibleForFullBenefits()) over writing a comment that says the same thing.

Some comments are worth writing - legal notices, informative or intent or clarification or warning or amplification comments, TODOs, and public-API javadocs - but the best comment is one you found a way not to write; clarifying comments risk being wrong and a TODO is no excuse for leaving bad code.

Avoid redundant, mandated, noise, and mumbling comments: they clutter the code, are less precise than the code itself, and any comment that forces the reader to look in another module to understand it has failed.
Do not mandate comments: a rule requiring a javadoc on every function or a comment on every variable just clutters code and breeds lies and misdirection.

Delete commented-out code and remove journal comments and authorship bylines; modern source-control systems remember the history and who changed what, so leaving them only accumulates cruft nobody dares delete.
Avoid closing-brace comments, position markers, and banners as navigation aids; shorten the functions instead, and use banners only very sparingly so they do not fade into noise.
If you must write a comment, describe only the nearby code with an obvious connection to it; do not include nonlocal or system-wide information, or arcane historical detail the reader does not need.

Choose a small set of formatting rules, apply them consistently, and on a team agree on one shared style enforced by an automated formatter rather than letting code look like the work of disagreeing individuals.
Formatting is about communication, the professional developer's first order of business; the readability and style of code outlive the current implementation and shape every future change.

Keep source files small: significant systems can be built from files typically around 200 lines with an upper limit near 500, and small files are usually easier to understand, though this is a strong preference rather than a hard rule.
Structure a source file like a newspaper article: a simple explanatory name, high-level concepts and algorithms at the top, and increasing detail as you read downward.
Use vertical openness and density: separate distinct concepts with blank lines, and keep tightly related lines vertically close together.

Keep closely related concepts vertically close: declare local variables near their use at the top of short functions, declare instance variables in one well-known place at the top of the class, and place a calling function above the function it calls so dependencies flow downward.
Keep lines short, with a limit around 100 to 120 characters, and avoid very long lines that force horizontal scrolling.
