Use horizontal whitespace to group strongly related tokens and separate weakly related ones, for example spaces around assignment operators but none between a function name and its opening parenthesis.
Do not column-align declarations or assignments; the alignment emphasizes the wrong axis and leads the eye astray, and a list long enough to tempt alignment is a signal the class should be split.
Indent code to make the scope hierarchy visible and never collapse scopes onto one line; when a loop has an empty body, make the dummy body visible with its own indented line and braces.
Keep variables private and resist automatically adding getters and setters, because pushing private variables out through accessors still exposes implementation.

Hiding implementation is about abstraction, not just a layer of functions: expose abstract interfaces that let callers manipulate the essence of the data without knowing its representation, so think hard about the best abstraction rather than blindly adding getters and setters.
Objects and data structures are near-opposites: objects hide their data behind abstractions and expose behavior, whereas data structures expose their data and have no significant behavior.

Procedural code makes it easy to add new functions but hard to add new data types, while OO code makes it easy to add new types but hard to add new functions; choose the style to fit the axis along which the system will grow.
condition: choice depends on whether the system more often needs new data types (favor objects/OO) or new functions (favor data structures and procedures)

statement: The idea that everything should be an object is a myth; sometimes simple data structures with procedures operating on them are the right choice.

Follow the Law of Demeter: a method should only call methods on its own class, on objects it creates, on its arguments, and on objects held in its instance variables - not on objects returned by those (talk to friends, not strangers).
exception: Does not apply to pure data structures, which legitimately expose their internal structure; Demeter constrains objects with behavior.

statement: Avoid train-wreck call chains such as a.getB().getC().getD(); split them into named intermediate steps.
condition: whether such a chain actually violates the Law of Demeter depends on whether the chained elements are objects or data structures

statement: Avoid hybrid structures that are half object and half data structure - significant behavior together with public variables or accessors that expose private data - because they make it hard to add either new functions or new data types and are the worst of both worlds.
Treat DTOs and Active Records as data structures: keep business-rule methods out of them and place those rules in separate objects that hide their data.

Error handling matters but must not obscure logic: if scattered error handling makes it hard to see what the code does, the design is wrong, so treat error handling as a separate concern viewable independently of the main logic.
Use exceptions rather than return codes or error flags so the caller's logic is not cluttered by immediate error checks and the algorithm and the error handling become separable concerns.

Write your try-catch-finally statement first: a try block defines a transaction-like scope whose catch must leave the program in a consistent state, so start from it (driven by tests that force exceptions) to define what callers should expect when things go wrong.

Prefer unchecked exceptions in general application code: checked exceptions violate the Open-Closed Principle by forcing a throws-clause cascade up the call chain that breaks encapsulation, and robust software is written without them in C#, C++, Python, and Ruby.
exception: Checked exceptions can be justified when writing a critical library whose callers must catch them.

statement: Provide context with every exception: include an informative message naming the failed operation and the type of failure, enough to locate and log the error, since a stack trace alone cannot convey intent.
Define exception classes by how they will be caught rather than by their source or type; often a single exception class per area of code suffices, with the message distinguishing the errors.
exception: Use distinct exception classes when you genuinely need to catch one type and let another pass through.

statement: Wrap third-party APIs at the boundary: wrapping minimizes your dependency on them, lets you switch libraries with little penalty, makes the calls easier to mock in tests, and lets you define an interface and exception types you control.

Use the Special Case pattern to remove exceptional-case clutter: return a configured object that handles the special case so the client code follows one clean path instead of branching on the exception.
Do not return null: returning null foists null-checks and NullPointerException risk onto callers, so return an empty collection, a special-case object, or throw an exception instead.
Do not pass null into methods: forbid passing null by default so that a null in an argument list signals a real problem, since most languages have no good way to handle an accidentally passed null.
exception: unless you are working with an API that explicitly expects null

statement: Do not pass a broad boundary interface such as Map around the system: wrap it inside a class or close family of classes and keep it out of public API signatures, so the boundary can evolve with minimal impact and the interface is tailored and harder to misuse.

Write learning tests to explore a third-party API in isolation: they cost nothing because you must learn the API anyway, and they pay back by catching behavioral changes when the package releases new versions.

Support every clean boundary with boundary tests that exercise the third-party interface the way production code does, and depend on something you control - a wrapper or an Adapter referenced in very few places - rather than scattering knowledge of third-party particulars through your code.

When you must use code you do not control or that does not yet exist, define the interface you wish you had and bridge to the real one with an Adapter, which keeps client code clean and gives a single place to change when the external API evolves.

The Three Laws of TDD: write no production code until you have a failing unit test; write no more of a unit test than is sufficient to fail (and not compiling is failing); write no more production code than is sufficient to pass the currently failing test.

Test code is just as important as production code and must be kept as clean; dirty tests are hard to change, become a liability that eventually gets discarded, and once the tests are gone the production code rots.

An automated suite of unit tests covering the production code is what keeps a design flexible, maintainable, and reusable, because high test coverage removes the fear that otherwise blocks programmers from changing and improving the code.
The most important quality of a clean test is readability - clarity, simplicity, and density of expression - so a test should say a lot with as few expressions as possible.
Structure each test in the Build-Operate-Check (given/when/then) form: build the test data, operate on it, then check that the operation produced the expected result.

Build a domain-specific testing language - a set of helper functions and utilities over the system APIs - that evolves by refactoring test code, to make tests more convenient to write and easier to read.
Test code lives under a dual standard: it may trade efficiency such as memory or CPU for clarity because it runs in a test environment, but it must never trade away cleanliness.
Minimize the number of asserts per test and test a single concept per test function rather than letting one test check several unrelated things.

Clean tests obey F.I.R.S.T.: Fast so they are run often, Independent so no test sets up another, Repeatable in any environment, Self-Validating with a boolean pass/fail, and Timely - written just before the production code that makes them pass.

Organize a class in a standard order: public static constants first, then private static variables, then private instance variables, then public functions, with each private utility placed just after the public function that calls it (the stepdown rule).

Keep variables and utility functions private, and loosen encapsulation to protected or package scope (for example so a test can reach them) only as a last resort after first looking for a way to keep them private.
Classes should be small, with size measured by counting responsibilities rather than lines; even a class with few methods is too big if it holds too many responsibilities.

A class name should describe its responsibilities; an ambiguous name with weasel words like Processor, Manager, or Super signals too many responsibilities, and you should be able to describe the class in about 25 words without using if, and, or, or but.
Apply the Single Responsibility Principle: a class or module should have one, and only one, reason to change.

Prefer many small, single-responsibility classes over a few large multipurpose ones; a system of small classes has no more moving parts to learn and lets a developer find things and understand only the complexity that is directly relevant.

Keep cohesion high: a class should have a small number of instance variables, each method should use one or more of them, and when cohesion drops because variables are used by only a subset of methods, split the class into more cohesive ones.

Breaking a large function into small ones tends to spawn new classes: promote the shared local variables to instance variables, then extract the cohesive subset into its own class, doing it as many tiny verified steps under a covering test suite rather than a rewrite.

Apply the Open-Closed Principle: structure classes to be open for extension but closed for modification, so new or changed features are added by extending the system (for example a new subclass) rather than editing existing, already-tested code.

Act on an SRP or structural problem when actual change forces you to open a class, not on speculation; if a class is logically complete and will not need changing for the foreseeable future, leave it alone.
condition: you find yourself needing to open the class to add or change behavior

statement: Apply the Dependency Inversion Principle: make classes depend on abstractions (interfaces) rather than concrete details, injecting the concrete implementation, which decouples the code, isolates it from change, and lets tests substitute a controllable test double.

Separate constructing a system from using it: keep the startup process that builds objects and wires dependencies apart from the runtime logic, because mixing them scatters the setup strategy, breaks the Single Responsibility Principle, and hampers testing.

Move construction to main (or modules main calls), with all dependency arrows pointing away from main, so the application assumes its objects are already built and wired and has no knowledge of the construction process.
Use the Abstract Factory pattern when the application must control when an object is created while keeping the details of that construction out of the application code.

Use Dependency Injection, the application of Inversion of Control to dependency management: an object stays passive and exposes constructor arguments or setters while an authoritative mechanism such as main or a DI container instantiates and injects its dependencies, honoring the Single Responsibility Principle.

It is a myth that a system can be built right the first time; implement only today's stories, then refactor and expand for tomorrow's, because software architectures can grow incrementally provided the proper separation of concerns is maintained.

Keep business logic in Plain-Old Java Objects free of framework dependencies and apply cross-cutting concerns (persistence, transactions, security) noninvasively via aspects or DI configuration, because tight coupling to a heavyweight container, as in EJB2, blocks isolated unit testing and reuse.

Avoid Big Design Up Front: start with a simple, decoupled architecture, deliver working stories quickly, and add infrastructure as you scale, because software (unlike a building) can be changed radically when its concerns are well separated.
A good architecture or API should largely disappear from view so the team spends its effort on user stories; over-engineered, invasive frameworks inhibit the efficient delivery of value.

Postpone decisions until the last responsible moment so you can decide with the most knowledge - customer feedback, reflection, and implementation experience - since a premature decision is made with suboptimal information.
Use standards wisely, only when they add demonstrable value, rather than adopting a strongly hyped standard when a lighter and more straightforward design would suffice.

Use Domain-Specific Languages where helpful to minimize the communication gap between a domain concept and the code that implements it, letting intent be expressed at the appropriate level of abstraction.
At every level of design, whether a whole system or a single module, use the simplest thing that can possibly work.
Kent Beck's four rules of Simple Design, in priority order: the design runs all the tests, contains no duplication, expresses the programmer's intent, and minimizes the number of classes and methods.

Making a system fully testable drives its design toward small, single-purpose classes with low coupling, because testable code naturally pushes you toward SRP, DIP, interfaces, and dependency injection.

Once tests exist, refactor incrementally - after each few lines of code, check whether you degraded the design and clean it up - because having the tests eliminates the fear that cleaning up the code will break it.

Eliminate duplication even at the level of a few lines; this reuse in the small shrinks system complexity and can reveal further abstractions, and the Template Method pattern removes higher-level duplication that differs only in one step.

Code should clearly express its author's intent through good names, small functions and classes, standard pattern nomenclature, and expressive tests, and the most important way to be expressive is to actually try rather than stopping once the code works.
Keep class and method counts low, but treat this as the lowest-priority Simple-Design rule and resist dogma such as creating an interface for every class or always separating data and behavior.
condition: this is the lowest priority of the four Simple Design rules, below tests, no-duplication, and expressiveness

statement: Concurrency is a decoupling strategy that separates what gets done from when it gets done, which can improve both throughput and the structure of an application and is warranted by genuine response-time or throughput needs.

Beware concurrency myths: concurrency does not always improve performance (only when there is shareable wait time), the design of a concurrent algorithm differs markedly from a single-threaded one, and using a Web or EJB container does not excuse you from guarding against concurrent-update and deadlock issues.
Correct concurrency is hard: it is complex even for simple problems, incurs performance and code overhead, and its bugs are usually not repeatable, so never dismiss a sporadic failure as a one-off.

Keep concurrency-related code separate from the rest of the code, because concurrency has its own development lifecycle and distinct challenges and is its own reason to change under the Single Responsibility Principle.

Severely limit the scope and access of any data that may be shared, keeping critical sections few, because more shared-update sites mean more chances to forget a guard, duplicate guarding effort (violating DRY), and obscure the source of failures.

Avoid sharing data where possible by using copies or read-only objects and merging results in a single thread, since the savings from avoiding a lock often outweigh the extra object-creation and garbage-collection cost.
Make threads as independent as possible, each working from unshared data held in local variables, so each thread behaves as if it were the only one in the world and needs no synchronization.

Know your concurrency library: prefer the provided thread-safe collections such as ConcurrentHashMap, an executor framework for unrelated tasks, and nonblocking solutions, and remember that several library classes are not thread-safe.

Learn the basic concurrency execution models - Producer-Consumer, Readers-Writers, and Dining Philosophers - and their solutions, because most concurrent problems you encounter are variations of these three.
Beware dependencies between synchronized methods and avoid using more than one method on a shared object, since synchronized only protects an individual method.
exception: When you must use more than one method on a shared object, make it correct with client-based locking, server-based locking, or an adapted-server intermediary.

statement: Keep synchronized sections as small as possible, because locks are expensive and extending a critical section beyond the minimum increases contention and degrades performance.

Writing correct graceful-shutdown code is hard, with common deadlocks where threads wait for a signal that never comes, so think about shutdown early, get it working early, and expect it to take longer than you think.

Test threaded code by writing tests that can expose problems and running them frequently across many programmatic and system configurations, platforms, and loads, tracking down every failure rather than writing it off as a one-off.

Get nonthreaded code working first by placing logic in thread-ignorant POJOs, then make the thread-aware code pluggable and tunable, run with more threads than processors and on every target platform, and instrument (jiggle) the code to force different orderings and surface rare flaws.
To write clean, well-structured code you must first write dirty code and then clean it; clean code is achieved by successive refinement through several drafts, not produced correct in a single pass.

Adding features to a poorly-abstracted structure degrades it rapidly (adding just two argument types turned a tidy class into a festering pile), so when you can see the structure will not stay maintainable, stop adding features and refactor before the mess grows too large to fix.

Do not improve a program with massive structural changes, which programs often never recover from; instead use TDD discipline to keep the system working at all times, making many tiny verified changes under a covering suite of unit and acceptance tests.

It is not enough for code to work; settling for merely working code is unprofessional, because bad code rots and ferments into a weight that drags the whole team down far more than bad schedules or requirements do.
Cleaning up rotted code later is expensive because modules accumulate hidden, tangled dependencies, whereas keeping code clean is cheap, so clean a mess immediately and never let the rot get started.

Professional code review - critiquing even good code in order to improve it - is a discipline every programmer should practice and welcome, because it is how we learn, just as doctors, pilots, and lawyers review each other's work.

Make it work before you make it right: before refactoring a class, raise its test coverage using a coverage tool and write your own independent unit tests, because you cannot safely refactor code you do not fully understand and that is not covered by tests.

C1 Inappropriate Information: a comment should not hold information better kept in source control, an issue tracker, or another record-keeping system (change histories, authors, dates); reserve comments for technical notes about the code and design.
C2 Obsolete Comment: a comment that has become old, irrelevant, or incorrect should be updated or deleted promptly, and it is best not to write a comment that will become obsolete.
C4 Poorly Written Comment: a comment worth writing is worth writing well - choose words carefully, use correct grammar, be brief, and do not ramble or state the obvious.

E1 Build Requires More Than One Step: building a project should be a single trivial operation - one command to check it out and one to build it - not a sequence of arcane commands or a hunt for scattered artifacts.
E2 Tests Require More Than One Step: you should be able to run all the unit tests with a single command or one button click, because running all the tests must be quick, easy, and obvious.

F4/G9/G12 Dead code and clutter: delete methods that are never called, statements that never execute (unreachable branches, empty catches), unused variables, empty default constructors, and other clutter, since source control remembers them and dead code rots out of sync with the design.
G1 Multiple Languages in One Source File: aim for one language per source file and take pains to minimize the number and extent of extra languages (XML, HTML, JavaScript) mixed into it.

G2 Obvious Behavior Is Unimplemented: following the Principle of Least Surprise, a function or class should implement the behaviors another programmer could reasonably expect (e.g. a day-name parser handling abbreviations and ignoring case), or readers lose trust in the names.
G3 Incorrect Behavior at the Boundaries: do not rely on intuition that code works - look for every boundary condition, corner case, and exception and write a test for it.

G4 Overridden Safeties: it is risky to override safety mechanisms - turning off compiler warnings or disabling failing tests with a promise to fix them later invites endless debugging, like the Chernobyl operators disabling safeties one by one.

G5 Duplication: every duplication is a missed abstraction - replace identical clumps with a method, a repeated switch/if-else over the same conditions with polymorphism, and similar-but-not-identical algorithms with the Template Method or Strategy pattern.

G6 Code at Wrong Level of Abstraction: separate higher-level general concepts from lower-level detail completely, placing each in the right container (base class versus derivative, or different files/modules); you cannot fake your way out of a misplaced abstraction.

G7 Base Classes Depending on Their Derivatives: in general a base class should know nothing about its derivatives, so the two can be deployed in independent components and a change to a derivative need not redeploy the base.
exception: Acceptable when the number of derivatives is strictly fixed and base and derivatives always deploy together, as in some finite state machines.

statement: G8 Too Much Information: keep interfaces tight and small to keep coupling low - hide data, utility functions, constants, and temporaries, and expose as few methods and instance variables as possible.

G11 Inconsistency: if you do something a certain way, do all similar things the same way (least surprise) - reuse variable names and method-naming patterns consistently so code is easier to read and modify.

G13 Artificial Coupling: do not couple things that do not depend on each other (e.g. a general enum nested in a specific class, or a general static function in a specific class); take the time to put each item where it belongs rather than where it is convenient.
G14 Feature Envy: a method should be interested in the data and functions of its own class, not reach into another object via accessors to manipulate that object's data.
exception: Feature Envy is sometimes a necessary evil, for example a report formatter that must read another object's data without coupling that object to the report format.

statement: G17 Misplaced Responsibility: place code where a reader would naturally expect it (least surprise), using the function names to decide - for example a total belongs in a getTotal function, and a constant belongs with the code that conceptually owns it.
G18 Inappropriate Static: prefer nonstatic methods, and make a function static only when there is no chance you would ever want it to behave polymorphically; when in doubt, make it nonstatic.

G19 Use Explanatory Variables: break calculations into intermediate values held in variables with meaningful names; more explanatory variables are generally better, and they can make an opaque module suddenly transparent.

G21 Understand the Algorithm: do not just plug in if statements and flags until the tests pass; understand how the function works and know the solution is correct, often by refactoring it until it is obvious.

G22 Make Logical Dependencies Physical: a dependent module should explicitly ask the module it depends on for what it needs rather than assuming it - for example, a reporter should query the formatter for the page size instead of hard-coding it.

G23 Prefer Polymorphism to If/Else or Switch/Case: consider polymorphism before reaching for a switch, since cases where functions vary more than types are rare; by the ONE SWITCH rule there should be at most one switch per type of selection, used to create the polymorphic objects.

G25 Replace Magic Numbers with Named Constants: hide raw numbers and any non-self-describing token (including strings like a test name) behind well-named constants such as SECONDS_PER_DAY or LINES_PER_PAGE.
exception: Very well-known, self-explanatory constants used with self-evident code (e.g. 5280 feet per mile, or radius times PI times 2) may remain raw.

statement: G26 Be Precise: make each decision precisely and handle its exceptions - check for null when a call might return it, use a locking mechanism when concurrent update is possible, use integers (or a Money class) for currency, and constrain types neither too much nor too little.

G27 Structure over Convention: enforce design decisions with structure rather than convention, because a base class with abstract methods forces compliance whereas a naming convention or a switch over named enums does not.

G28 Encapsulate Conditionals: extract a well-named function that expresses the intent of a conditional, so that for example if (shouldBeDeleted(timer)) replaces if (timer.hasExpired() && !timer.isRecurrent()).
G29 Avoid Negative Conditionals: express conditionals as positives where possible, since a negative is a bit harder to understand than the equivalent positive.

G31 Hidden Temporal Couplings: when calls must happen in a certain order, make the coupling explicit by structuring each function to produce a result the next one needs (a bucket brigade), so the calls cannot be made out of order.

G32 Don't Be Arbitrary: have a reason for the way you structure code and communicate it through the structure, because an arbitrary-looking structure invites others to change it - for example a public class that is not a utility of another should not be nested inside it.

G33 Encapsulate Boundary Conditions: handle boundary arithmetic in one place behind a named variable (for example nextLevel = level + 1) instead of scattering raw +1 and -1 expressions through the code.

G35 Keep Configurable Data at High Levels: keep a known default or configuration constant at a high level of abstraction and pass it down as an argument, rather than burying it in a low-level function where it is hard to find and change.

J1-J3 Java specifics: import a whole package with a wildcard rather than maintaining a long explicit import list, do not inherit constants through an interface (import them statically instead), and prefer enums to integer or string constants when modeling a fixed set of values.

N7 Names Should Describe Side-Effects: a name should reveal everything the function does, including side effects, so a getter that also creates the object on first access should be named something like createOrReturn rather than a bare get.
T1 Insufficient Tests: a test suite should test everything that could possibly break, not just whatever is convenient; a passing suite that leaves much of the code unexercised is insufficient.
T2 Use a Coverage Tool: use a coverage tool to find the gaps in your testing, since such tools make it easy to see which statements and branches your tests do not exercise.
T3 Don't Skip Trivial Tests: write the trivial tests too, because they are easy to write and their documentary value is higher than the cost to produce them.

T4 An Ignored Test Is a Question about an Ambiguity: when a requirement is unclear, express the question as a commented-out or @Ignore-annotated test, choosing between them based on whether the ambiguity would still compile.
T6 Exhaustively Test Near Bugs: bugs tend to congregate, so when you find a bug in a function, do an exhaustive test of that function because the bug is probably not alone.

T7/T8 Patterns are revealing: complete, sensibly ordered test cases expose patterns in how tests fail, and looking at which code the passing tests do or do not execute gives clues to why the failing tests fail.

Clean code is not produced by following a list of rules or memorizing heuristics; the heuristics merely imply a value system, and professionalism and craftsmanship come from values that drive disciplines.

Prefer server-based locking over client-based locking for a shared object, because putting the lock in the server removes repeated client code, reduces the chance a client forgets to lock, enforces a single policy in one place, and narrows the scope of the shared variables; if you do not own the server, wrap it with an Adapter that adds the locking.
Deadlock requires four conditions to hold simultaneously - mutual exclusion, lock-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait - so breaking any one of these conditions makes deadlock impossible.

To prevent deadlock, break one of its four conditions: imposing a global resource-acquisition order to break circular wait is the most common and usually only needs a convention; alternatives are allowing simultaneous use or adding resources (mutual exclusion), releasing all and restarting when a resource is busy (lock-and-wait, but risks starvation and livelock), or letting threads request release (preemption).
Refactoring (noun) is a change to the internal structure of software that makes it easier to understand and cheaper to modify without altering its observable behavior.
Refactoring (verb) is restructuring software by applying a series of small refactorings without changing its observable behavior.
Refactoring proceeds as a sequence of small behavior-preserving steps composed into a large change, so the code spends little time in a broken state and the work can be stopped at any point.
If a codebase is left broken for days during what is called refactoring, the work was not actually refactoring.
When a feature must be added to code that is not structured conveniently for it, first refactor to make the change easy, then make the change.
A poorly designed system is hard to change because it is difficult to find what to change and to predict how changes interact, which raises the chance of introducing bugs.
When code lacks structure, it is usually easier to add the missing structure first and then make the intended change.
In a long-lived program, duplicated code is a liability because every copy must be changed consistently.
exception: If the program will never change again, copy-and-paste duplication is acceptable.

statement: The need to understand or change code is what justifies refactoring it; code that works and never needs to be understood or changed can be left alone.
condition: Someone needs to understand or modify the code.

statement: Before starting to refactor, ensure a solid suite of tests exists for the section of code being changed.
Refactoring tests must be self-checking, reporting pass or fail automatically rather than requiring manual comparison of values.
A test suite acts as a bug detector during refactoring: expressing intent twice (in code and in the test) means an error must be made consistently in both places to escape detection.
Compile and run the tests after every refactoring step, however trivial, so that any mistake is isolated to a small recent change.
The essence of refactoring is making small changes and testing after each one, which keeps a tight feedback loop and avoids long debugging episodes.
Because refactoring changes a program in small steps, a mistake is easy to localize to the step that introduced it.
Commit to a local version-control system after each successful refactoring so it is easy to return to a working state, and squash into larger commits before pushing to a shared repository.
If a test fails during refactoring and the cause is not immediately obvious, revert to the last good commit and redo the work in smaller steps.
Small refactoring steps let you move faster because they compose well and eliminate time spent debugging.
To capture an insight about a block of code, apply Extract Function and name the new function after what it does, moving the understanding from your head into the code.
When extracting a function, variables that are read but not modified can be passed as parameters, while a variable that is modified can be returned.
Remove local and temporary variables before doing extractions, because temporaries create locally scoped names that complicate breaking a function apart.
Apply Replace Temp with Query to eliminate a temporary variable that is computed from other accessible data.
Good programmers write code that humans can understand, not merely code that a computer can execute.
Good code communicates its intent clearly, variable and function names are central to that clarity, and names should be changed freely whenever a clearer one is found.
Breaking a large function into smaller ones only adds value if the smaller functions are well named; settle for the best current name and rename later when a better one emerges.

Most programmers, even experienced ones, are poor judges of how code actually performs, because intuition is broken by compilers and caching, and performance usually depends on only a few parts of the code.
While refactoring, generally ignore performance; if a refactoring introduces a slowdown, finish refactoring first and tune afterward, because well-factored code is easier to tune.
Prefer to treat data as immutable as much as possible, because widespread mutable state quickly becomes a source of defects.
Apply Split Phase to divide logic into one phase that computes an intermediate data structure and a second phase that renders or consumes it.
Apply Replace Conditional with Polymorphism to turn type-based switch logic into a subclass hierarchy that dispatches polymorphically.
condition: Multiple functions branch on the same type code, so the approach grows more valuable as that number increases.

statement: Type-based conditional logic tends to decay as further modifications are made unless it is reinforced by structural language features such as polymorphism.
condition: The conditional is not reinforced by structural elements.

statement: Adding code is justified when the extra structure separates concerns and improves clarity, since clarity, not brevity, is what makes software easy to evolve.
Follow the campsite rule: always leave the codebase healthier than you found it.
Separate the two hats of development: when adding functionality do not restructure existing code, and when refactoring do not add functionality or new tests except to accommodate interface changes.
The real measure of code quality is how easily the code can be changed.

Refactoring and performance optimization both manipulate code without changing functionality, but refactoring always aims to make code easier to understand and cheaper to modify, whereas optimization aims only at speed and may accept harder-to-work-with code.
Observable behavior is preserved in the user-visible sense: call-stack and performance characteristics and module interfaces may change, and latent unobserved bugs may even be fixed.
condition: Behavior is judged by what the user should care about, not exact internal behavior.

statement: Without refactoring, the internal design of software decays cumulatively, because changes made for short-term goals without full comprehension of the architecture erode its structure.
Eliminating duplicated code is a central aspect of improving design, because saying everything once and only once makes the system easier to modify correctly.
The most important reader of source code is the future human who must modify it (often yourself); refactoring makes code communicate its purpose to that reader.
Refactoring helps find bugs, because deeply understanding code in order to refactor it surfaces hidden assumptions and makes defects visible.

By the Design Stamina Hypothesis, investing in good internal design increases the stamina of the effort, letting a team go faster for longer; good modularity means understanding only a small subset of the code to make a change.
By the Rule of Three, refactor to remove duplication the third time you do something similar.

Use preparatory refactoring: just before adding a feature, restructure the code so the feature becomes easy to add (for example Parameterize Function instead of copying a function and changing literals).
When fixing a bug, refactor to unify the duplicated or tangled code that caused it, which increases the chance the fix stays fixed and fewer related bugs appear.
Use comprehension refactoring: whenever you must stop and think to understand code, refactor (rename, decompose) to make that understanding immediately apparent and preserved for colleagues.

Use litter-pickup refactoring: when you see code doing something badly, fix it immediately if easy, otherwise note it; small improvements on each pass fix it over time without ever leaving the code broken.
Most refactoring should be opportunistic, woven into adding a feature or fixing a bug, not scheduled as a separate activity.
Even excellent code needs continual refactoring, because the design tradeoffs that were right for past features may no longer fit new ones; software should never be considered done.
For each desired change, first make the change easy (which may itself be hard), then make the easy change.
Planned, dedicated refactoring episodes should be rare; they are warranted mainly when a team has neglected refactoring and must get the codebase into shape for upcoming features.
condition: The team has accumulated neglect that opportunistic refactoring cannot absorb.

statement: Separating refactoring and feature changes into different commits is not a self-evident principle; it is only worthwhile if it actually makes review and life easier, so teams should experiment.

For long-term refactoring, prefer gradual migration over a dedicated effort; for example, use Branch By Abstraction to introduce an abstraction over either the old or new library, then switch callers incrementally.

Code reviews spread knowledge and improve clarity, and refactoring during review makes suggestions concrete and surfaces deeper ideas; reviews work best with the original author present, the logical conclusion being pair programming.
Justify refactoring on economic grounds: it is done because it makes a team faster to add features and fix bugs, not for moral or aesthetic 'clean code' reasons.
Do not refactor code you do not need to modify; ugly code that can be treated as a stable API can stay ugly until you actually need to understand how it works.
condition: You do not need to understand or change the code.

statement: Sometimes rewriting code is better than refactoring it; this is a judgment call requiring experience and often cannot be decided without first attempting the refactoring.

A published interface is one used by clients independent of those who declare it; renaming such a function requires retaining the old declaration as a pass-through (and deprecating it), which complicates the interface but avoids breaking clients.
condition: The interface is published / consumed by code you cannot change in the same commit.

statement: Prefer team ownership of code over fine-grained strong code ownership, because ownership boundaries force breaking-change workarounds; individual responsibility should mean monitoring changes, not blocking them by default.
The difficulty of integrating a feature branch grows worse than linearly with its age because of semantic merge conflicts that text-based version control cannot detect.
Prefer Continuous Integration (trunk-based development) with each member integrating to mainline at least daily, which keeps branches from diverging and greatly reduces merge complexity.

Continuous Integration is far more compatible with refactoring than long feature branches, because refactorings make many small changes across the codebase that are especially prone to semantic merge conflicts.
Realistic refactoring requires self-testing code: a comprehensive test suite that runs fast enough to be run frequently, so a mistake is caught while only a few lines have changed.

If an environment provides provably-safe automated refactorings, those can be trusted even without running tests, which is a useful fallback for codebases with poor test coverage, at the cost of a limited set of available refactorings.
condition: Only refactorings that are safely automated are used.

statement: You cannot safely refactor a large legacy system that has no tests; the route is to first get it under test by finding seams where tests can be inserted (per Working Effectively with Legacy Code), accepting that creating seams is riskier refactoring done without tests.
condition: The legacy system lacks adequate tests.

statement: Do not try to refactor a complicated legacy mess into clean code all at once; improve it in pieces as you pass through, doing more refactoring in areas you visit frequently for a bigger payoff.

Refactor a database by combining schema and access-code changes with small, composable data-migration scripts, each capturing a complete change so the system still runs, and spreading database changes over multiple releases (parallel change / expand-contract).

Prefer evolutionary design (YAGNI): build software that excellently solves only the currently understood needs and use refactoring to adapt as needs change, rather than adding speculative flexibility mechanisms that usually slow reaction to change.
Add a flexibility mechanism now only if refactoring it in later would be substantially harder; mechanisms that do not increase complexity (such as small, well-named functions) can be included freely.
condition: Later refactoring to add the flexibility would be substantially harder than adding it now.

statement: Self-testing code, continuous integration, and refactoring form a mutually reinforcing trio (from Extreme Programming) that enables the YAGNI design approach and continuous delivery.

The secret to fast software, outside hard real-time contexts, is to write well-factored tunable software first and then tune it for sufficient speed, because well-factored code is more amenable to performance tuning.
condition: The system is not a hard real-time system, which may instead require time budgeting.

statement: The constant-attention approach of optimizing everywhere all the time works poorly, because improvements are spread thin, made with a narrow view of behavior, and usually make code harder to work with without making it faster.
In most programs most of the execution time is spent in a small fraction of the code, so optimizing all code equally wastes roughly ninety percent of the effort.

During performance optimization, measure with a profiler rather than speculate, focus on the hot spots, change in small steps, and after each step compile, test, and re-profile, backing out any change that does not improve performance.
To refactor reliably, a tool must operate on the code's syntax tree rather than its text, and static typing makes many refactorings such as renaming completely safe and automatic.
Deciding when to refactor and when to stop is as important as the mechanics, and no set of metrics rivals informed human intuition; code smells are indicators of trouble, not precise criteria.

Mysterious Name smell: names must clearly communicate intent, so rename aggressively (Change Function Declaration, Rename Variable, Rename Field); being unable to find a good name is often a sign of a deeper design problem.

Duplicated Code smell: unify repeated code structure with Extract Function, use Slide Statements to align near-identical fragments for extraction, and Pull Up Method when duplicates are in sibling subclasses.

Long Function smell: short, well-named functions live best; be aggressive about decomposing, and whenever you feel the urge to write a comment, instead extract a function named after the intention of the code.

To shorten a long function, mostly use Extract Function; remove temporaries with Replace Temp with Query, slim parameters with Introduce Parameter Object or Preserve Whole Object, and handle conditionals and loops with Decompose Conditional, Replace Conditional with Polymorphism, and Split Loop.
Long Parameter List smell: reduce parameters with Replace Parameter with Query, Preserve Whole Object, Introduce Parameter Object, Remove Flag Argument, and Combine Functions into Class.

Global Data smell: global data is dangerous because it can be modified from anywhere with no way to discover what changed it; the first defense is Encapsulate Variable, then narrow its scope; it is worst when mutable, while guaranteed-immutable global data is relatively safe.
exception: Global data guaranteed never to change after startup is relatively safe.

statement: Mutable Data smell: data changes cause unexpected coupling and hard-to-find bugs, so limit updates with Encapsulate Variable, Split Variable, Separate Query from Modifier, Remove Setting Method, and Replace Derived Variable with Query; the risk grows as the variable's scope grows.

Divergent Change smell: when one module is changed in different ways for different reasons, split the separate contexts into separate modules using Split Phase, Move Function, or Extract Class so each change touches one context.

Shotgun Surgery smell: when one change forces many little edits across many classes, gather the scattered logic into one module with Move Function, Move Field, Combine Functions into Class or Transform, or by inlining and then re-extracting.

Feature Envy smell: when a function interacts more with another module's data than with its own, move it to the data with Move Function; the rule of thumb is to put together things that change together, and data and the behavior that uses it usually change together.
exception: Patterns such as Strategy and Visitor deliberately separate behavior from data to ease changing behavior.

statement: Data Clumps smell: when the same group of data items recurs together, extract them into a class (Extract Class, Introduce Parameter Object, Preserve Whole Object); a good test is whether deleting one value would leave the others meaningless.

Primitive Obsession smell: reluctance to create domain types (money, ranges, phone numbers) leads to stringly-typed code; use Replace Primitive with Object, and for a type code controlling behavior use Replace Type Code with Subclasses followed by Replace Conditional with Polymorphism.

Repeated Switches smell: the problem is the same switching logic duplicated in many places (not conditionals in general), which forces updating every switch when a clause is added; replace it with Replace Conditional with Polymorphism.
Loops smell: replace explicit loops with first-class pipeline operations such as filter and map via Replace Loop with Pipeline, which makes the processing easier to follow.
Lazy Element smell: a function or class that does not earn its own structure should be removed by inlining (Inline Function, Inline Class, or Collapse Hierarchy).

Speculative Generality smell: unused hooks and abstractions added in case they are someday needed should be removed (Collapse Hierarchy, Inline Function/Class, Change Function Declaration to drop unused parameters, Remove Dead Code); it is often spotted when the only users of an element are test cases.

Temporary Field smell: a field set only in certain circumstances is confusing; give the orphan fields a home with Extract Class and Move Function, and use Introduce Special Case to remove the conditional code.
Message Chains smell: a client navigating object to object becomes coupled to the navigation structure; use Hide Delegate, or Extract Function and Move Function to push the using-code down the chain.

Middle Man smell: when a class delegates most of its interface to another, use Remove Middle Man to talk to the real object directly, Inline Function for the few trivial delegators, or Replace Superclass/Subclass with Delegate to fold in added behavior.
Insider Trading smell: modules trading too much data increase coupling; reduce it with Move Function and Move Field, a shared third module, or Hide Delegate to act as an intermediary.

Large Class smell: a class doing too much shows up as too many fields and breeds duplicated code; split it with Extract Class, Extract Superclass, or Replace Type Code with Subclasses, using common field prefixes and the subset of features each client uses as clues for the split.

Alternative Classes with Different Interfaces smell: to let one class substitute for another, make their interfaces match using Change Function Declaration and Move Function, and use Extract Superclass if matching creates duplication.

Data Class smell: a class with only fields and accessors is a dumb data holder whose behavior usually belongs elsewhere; encapsulate public fields (Encapsulate Record), apply Remove Setting Method to fields that should not change, and move behavior in with Move Function or Extract Function.
exception: An immutable result record (such as the intermediate structure from Split Phase) is a legitimate data class and need not be encapsulated.

statement: Refused Bequest smell: a subclass refusing inherited implementation is usually a faint smell not worth cleaning, but if it refuses the superclass interface the smell is strong and the hierarchy should be replaced with delegation (Replace Subclass with Delegate or Replace Superclass with Delegate).
condition: Act on the inherited-implementation case only when it causes real confusion or problems.

statement: Comments smell: comments are often used as deodorant for bad code, so when you feel the need to write one, first try to refactor (Extract Function, rename via Change Function Declaration, or Introduce Assertion) so the comment becomes superfluous; legitimate comments explain why something is done or flag uncertainty.
Most programming time is spent debugging — finding bugs — rather than writing code, so self-testing code that catches bugs early sharply increases programmer effectiveness.
Make all tests fully automatic and self-checking, so they compare actual against expected results and report a simple pass or fail without manual inspection.
A suite of tests run frequently is a powerful bug detector, because a newly failing test points to the small amount of code changed since the suite last passed.

Write tests before the code (Test-Driven Development): write a failing test, write code to make it pass, then refactor, cycling many times per hour; this focuses attention on the interface and gives a clear point at which the work is done.
Make sure each test can fail when it should, for example by temporarily injecting a fault and confirming the test goes red, so you trust the test actually exercises the code.
Run the tests that exercise the code you are working on at least every few minutes, and run the whole suite at least daily.
Never refactor on a red bar: do not refactor while any test is failing, and when a change breaks tests, revert to the last all-passing (green) state rather than debugging forward.

Testing should be risk-driven and aimed at finding bugs: concentrate on the areas and complex code most likely to fail, do not bother testing trivial accessors, and prefer running incomplete tests over not running complete ones.

Build a fresh test fixture before each test (for example in a beforeEach hook) to keep tests isolated, because a shared mutable fixture causes tests to interact and fail nondeterministically depending on run order.
exception: A shared fixture is acceptable only when it is genuinely immutable or creation is too slow to repeat.

statement: As a general rule keep a single verify (assertion) per test, because a test stops at the first failed assertion and later assertions can hide useful diagnostic information.

Think about the boundary conditions under which things might go wrong — empty collections, zero, negative, blank, and wrong-typed inputs — and concentrate tests there, actively trying to break your own code.

Because refactoring need only preserve observable behavior, behavior outside the observable bounds (such as an unanticipated error) need not be preserved, and a test pinning such behavior can be discarded before refactoring.

Validate inputs that arrive from an external source and test that validation, but avoid duplicate validation checks between modules within the same codebase, which can cause more trouble than they are worth.
condition: The input crosses a trust boundary from outside the codebase.

statement: Use Introduce Assertion to fail fast on a condition that could otherwise spread bad data through the program; assertions are themselves a form of test and need no separate test.
Do not let the fact that testing cannot catch every bug stop you from writing tests that catch most; there are diminishing returns, so concentrate effort where the risk and complexity are highest.
When you get a bug report, first write a unit test that exposes the bug and only then fix it, so the bug stays dead and the gap in the suite is closed.

Test coverage is useful only for finding untested areas of code, not for assessing the quality of a test suite; the best measure of an adequate suite is the subjective confidence that an introduced defect would trip some test.
Over-testing is possible (a sign is spending more time changing tests than the code under test), but it is vanishingly rare compared with under-testing.
Separate business logic from user-interface, persistence, and external-service code so the logic can be reasoned about and tested in isolation.
Each refactoring's mechanics emphasize the safe way: take very small steps and test after every one, and the trickier the situation the smaller the steps should be.

Apply Extract Function on the criterion of separating intention from implementation: if you must spend effort to work out what a fragment of code does, extract it into a function named after that intent; the deciding factor is the semantic distance between what and how, not the function's length.
exception: If you cannot find a name more meaningful than the code itself, that is a sign not to extract it.

statement: Apply Inline Function when a function's body is as clear as its name, to remove needless indirection, or to gather a badly factored group of functions into one place before re-extracting; do not inline when it would be complicated (for example recursion, multiple return points, or a polymorphic method).
exception: Do not inline a polymorphic method or where recursion or multiple return points make it complicated.

statement: Apply Extract Variable to give a name to a complex sub-expression so its purpose is understandable; if the name is meaningful beyond the current function, prefer a function (Extract Function) so the expression is reusable and reduces duplication, and ensure the expression has no side effects.
Apply Inline Variable when a variable's name communicates no more than the expression it holds, or when the variable gets in the way of refactoring the surrounding code.

Treat function declarations as the joints of a system: a good name lets a reader understand a call without reading the body, so fix a misleading name as soon as a better one is known, and choose parameters to widen a function's applicability and reduce coupling rather than by fixed rules.
When changing the declaration of a published API, pause after creating the new function, deprecate the old one as a pass-through, and remove it only once all clients have migrated.
condition: The function is a published API used by code you cannot change yourself.

statement: Apply Encapsulate Variable to route all access to widely-scoped or mutable data through functions, which turns the hard problem of moving data into the easier one of reorganizing functions and provides a single point to add validation or monitoring; the greater the data's scope, the more important this is.
exception: Encapsulation matters much less for immutable data, which can be freely copied and needs no update hooks.

statement: Apply Rename Variable when a variable's name does not clearly explain its purpose; the importance of getting the name right scales with how widely the variable is used, so persistent fields deserve the most care and short-lived locals the least.

Apply Introduce Parameter Object when a group of data items regularly travel together (a data clump): replace them with a single structure, which makes their relationship explicit, shrinks parameter lists, and creates a new abstraction that behavior can be gathered around.

Apply Combine Functions into Class when a group of functions operate closely on a common body of data, to make the shared environment explicit and simplify calls; prefer a class over nested functions because nested functions are harder to test and a class can expose several functions to collaborators.

Apply Combine Functions into Transform to bring repeated derivation calculations into one transform that computes all derived values into output fields, giving a single place to find and update them; use a class instead when the source data is updated, because derived data stored by a transform would go stale.
exception: If the source data gets updated in place, use Combine Functions into Class so derivations stay consistent.

statement: Apply Split Phase when one piece of code deals with two different things, dividing it into two sequential phases connected by a clear intermediate data structure, so each phase can be understood and changed independently.

Favor objects over bare records for mutable data (Encapsulate Record), because an object hides which fields are stored versus computed and makes renaming easier by serving both old and new names during migration; a plain immutable record needs no such encapsulation.
exception: For immutable data a plain record is acceptable and need not be encapsulated.

statement: When encapsulating a collection, do not let the getter return the raw collection (clients could mutate it without the owner's knowledge); provide add and remove modifier methods on the owning class and return a copy or read-only view.

Apply Replace Primitive with Object as soon as a simple data item (such as a phone number held as a string) needs behavior beyond simple printing, wrapping it in its own class to give that behavior a home and avoid duplicated logic; it is considered one of the most valuable refactorings.

Apply Replace Temp with Query to a temporary variable that is computed once and thereafter only read, turning it into a query function, which eases extraction by removing variables to pass and removes duplicated calculation; it works best inside a class that provides shared context.
condition: The variable is assigned once and only read afterward; outside a class a top-level query may take too many parameters to be worthwhile.

statement: Apply Extract Class when a class has grown too big to understand easily, splitting where a subset of data and methods belong together — good signs are data that changes together or fields and methods that would become nonsense if one piece were removed.

Apply Inline Class to a class that no longer pulls its weight, folding it into the class that uses it most; it is also useful to merge two classes into one before using Extract Class to re-split them with a better allocation of features.

Apply Hide Delegate when client code reaches through a server object's field to call a delegate: add a delegating method on the server so that changes to the delegate's interface propagate only to the server and not to every client.

Apply Remove Middle Man when a server class delegates so many methods that it is mostly a pass-through, letting clients call the delegate directly; the right amount of hiding shifts over time, so adjust between Hide Delegate and Remove Middle Man as the system changes.

Apply Substitute Algorithm when you find a clearer way to do something, replacing the whole algorithm; first decompose the method as much as possible, because substituting a large complex algorithm is only tractable once it is simple.
condition: The method has been decomposed enough that the substitution is tractable.

statement: Apply Move Function to relocate a function into the module or class whose elements it references most (or toward its callers), which improves modularity and encapsulation by reducing other parts' dependence on this module's details.

A program's strength rests on its data structures, so apply Move Field as soon as you realize a field lives in the wrong record — for example data always passed together with another, or that changes together — because leaving bad data structures in place confuses thinking and complicates code far into the future.
Apply Move Statements into Function when the same code runs every time a particular function is called, folding it into the function so future modifications happen in one place.

Apply Move Statements to Callers when behavior that was once cohesive within a function now needs to vary for some of its calls, moving the varying statements out to the callers so they can be changed independently.

Apply Replace Inline Code with Function Call when inline code does the same thing as an existing function (especially a library function), replacing it with a call so future changes happen in one place; do not do this when the similarity is coincidental and you would not want both to change together.
exception: If the similarity is coincidental, so the inline code should not change when the function changes, do not replace it.

statement: Apply Slide Statements to keep related code together — for example declaring a variable just before its first use rather than at the top of a function — often as a preparatory step that makes an Extract Function possible.

Apply Split Loop to a loop doing two different things so each concern is in its own loop and can be understood and modified independently; do not avoid it for fear of two passes, because iteration is rarely the bottleneck and refactoring should be separated from optimization.

Apply Replace Loop with Pipeline to express collection processing as a series of operations such as map and filter instead of an explicit loop, because the logic then reads top to bottom as objects flow through the pipeline.
Apply Remove Dead Code to delete unused code rather than commenting it out, because version control can recover it if ever needed and unused code is a real burden on understanding the software.

Apply Split Variable when a variable is assigned more than once and thus carries more than one responsibility, giving each responsibility its own single-assignment variable; loop variables and accumulating variables are the legitimate exceptions that are assigned repeatedly.
exception: Loop variables and collecting/accumulator variables legitimately receive multiple assignments and should not be split.

statement: Apply Rename Field to keep data-structure field names (and the getters and setters that stand in for them) clear, because data structures are the key to understanding a program, and rename them as your understanding improves, especially when they are widely used.

Apply Replace Derived Variable with Query to replace a mutable variable that could be recalculated with a query, minimizing the scope of mutable data and avoiding corruption when the source changes; a reasonable exception is keeping stored derived data when the source data is immutable or the derived data is very transient.
exception: Keep stored derived data when its source is immutable (and the result can be made immutable) or the derived data is very transient.

statement: Apply Change Reference to Value to make a nested object an immutable Value Object — replaced wholesale on change — when it should be easy to reason about, copied freely, or used across distributed and concurrent systems; do not, when the object must be shared so that a change is visible to all its collaborators, in which case keep it a reference.
exception: If the object must be shared so a change is visible to all collaborators, keep it a reference rather than a value.

statement: Apply Change Value to Reference when several records represent the same logical entity and that entity needs to be updated: turn the copies into a single shared reference (usually via a repository) so any change is visible everywhere and missed copies cannot cause inconsistency.
condition: The shared logical data needs to be updated; if it never changes, copies are acceptable.

statement: Apply Decompose Conditional to complex conditional logic by extracting the condition and each branch into functions named after their intent, so the code communicates why it branches rather than only what it does.

Apply Consolidate Conditional Expression when several different checks all lead to the same action, combining them with and/or into a single check (often setting up an Extract Function); do not consolidate checks that are genuinely independent and should not be thought of as one.
exception: If the checks are truly independent and should not be read as a single combined check, do not consolidate them.

statement: Apply Replace Nested Conditional with Guard Clauses when one leg of a conditional is an unusual or exceptional case: check it and return early as a guard clause, reserving if/else for two equally-weighted normal legs; the single-exit-point rule is not useful, so let clarity decide.

Apply Replace Conditional with Polymorphism to add structure to complex conditional logic — especially when several functions switch on the same type code, or there is a base case with variants — but do not replace all conditional logic with polymorphism, because basic conditionals are perfectly appropriate.
exception: Do not convert ordinary, simple conditional logic to polymorphism; reserve it for type-based or base-plus-variant cases.

statement: Apply Introduce Special Case when many users of a data structure check for a particular value and then react the same way: capture that common reaction in a special-case object and replace the checks with calls; the Null Object pattern is the special case of this for null values.

Apply Introduce Assertion to make an assumption that a section of code depends on explicit; an assertion failure signals a programmer error, must never be relied upon for normal control flow, and the program must behave identically if all assertions are removed — their main lasting value is communicating the assumed program state.
exception: Assertions must not be used for normal control flow or relied on by other parts of the system; the program must run correctly with all assertions removed.

statement: Apply Parameterize Function when two functions carry out the same logic with different literal values, merging them into one function that takes those values as parameters and is therefore usable in more contexts.

Apply Remove Flag Argument to replace a flag argument (a literal the caller sets to select which logic runs) with explicit, separately named functions, because flag arguments hide which calls are available and boolean flags do not convey their meaning; an argument only counts as a flag when callers pass a literal and the implementation uses it for control flow rather than as data passed onward.

Apply Preserve Whole Object when code derives several values from a record only to pass them into a function: pass the whole record instead, which copes better if the function later needs more of the record and shrinks the parameter list; do not, when you do not want the callee coupled to the whole object, typically across module boundaries.
exception: Do not pass the whole object when you want to avoid coupling the called function to it, typically when they live in different modules.

statement: Apply Replace Parameter with Query when a caller passes a value the function could just as easily determine for itself, removing the parameter so callers are simpler; do not, when removing it would add an unwanted dependency to the function body.
exception: Do not remove the parameter if doing so forces the function body to take on a dependency you would rather it not have.

statement: Apply Replace Query with Parameter when a function body references an element in its scope you want it independent of (such as a global or a soon-to-move element), replacing the internal reference with a parameter to gain referential transparency, while balancing against overly long parameter lists.

Apply Remove Setting Method (and make the field immutable) when a field should not change after construction, which makes that intent clear; this commonly arises when accessors are used even inside constructors or when objects are built by a creation script.

Prefer a factory function over a raw constructor (Replace Constructor with Factory Function) when you need to return a subclass or proxy, give the creation a clearer name, or call it where a normal function is expected, since constructors carry those fixed limitations.

Apply Replace Function with Command only when you specifically need a facility a plain function cannot provide — such as undo, parameters built up in stages, inheritance and hooks, or breaking a complex function into methods in a language lacking nested functions; given the choice, pick a plain first-class function about ninety-five percent of the time because a command costs extra complexity.
exception: Use a command only for a capability a simpler function or approach cannot provide.

statement: Apply Replace Command with Function to turn a command object back into a regular function when the computation is not complex enough to justify the command object's overhead.

Apply Pull Up Method to remove duplicate methods across sibling subclasses by moving a common method into the superclass; look for the differences first because they often reveal behavior you forgot to test, and pull up any subclass-only fields or methods it references beforehand.
Apply Pull Up Field to move duplicate fields that are used the same way across subclasses into the superclass, which removes the duplicate declaration and lets field-using behavior move up too.

Apply Pull Up Constructor Body to move common subclass constructor behavior into the superclass constructor; if this becomes messy because of constructor ordering rules, switch to Replace Constructor with Factory Function.

Apply Push Down Method to move a method that is only relevant to one or a few subclasses out of the superclass and onto those subclasses; this is only valid when callers know they are working with the specific subclass, otherwise use Replace Conditional with Polymorphism.
condition: Callers know the concrete subclass they are working with.

statement: Apply Push Down Field to move a field used only by one or a few subclasses out of the superclass and onto those subclasses.

Apply Replace Type Code with Subclasses when a type code drives conditional behavior in several functions (enabling Replace Conditional with Polymorphism) or when some fields or methods are valid only for particular type-code values (enabling Push Down Field); a plain type code is sufficient otherwise.
condition: There is type-dependent behavior or type-specific fields; a bare type code suffices when neither applies.

statement: Apply Remove Subclass to a subclass that has come to do too little, replacing it with a field on the superclass, because it now costs more in understanding than the variation it expresses.

Apply Extract Superclass when two classes do similar things, pulling the similarities up with Pull Up Field and Pull Up Method; inheritance can be discovered during a program's evolution rather than only planned in advance, and Extract Superclass is often the simpler first choice over Extract Class because you can later Replace Superclass with Delegate.
Apply Collapse Hierarchy to merge a class with its parent when, after moving features around, the two are no longer different enough to be worth keeping separate.

Apply Replace Subclass with Delegate when you need to vary behavior on more than one axis (inheritance can express only a single axis) or to avoid the tight coupling between parent and child, reflecting the principle of favoring object composition over class inheritance.

Apply Replace Superclass with Delegate when functions of the superclass do not make sense on the subclass, or when not every instance of the subclass is a valid instance of the superclass (the type-instance homonym mistake): make the would-be superclass a field and delegate only the operations that apply.
condition: Inheritance is being used for reuse even though the subclass is not a true subtype of the superclass.

statement: Clients should depend on abstract interfaces rather than concrete implementation classes (program to an interface, not an implementation).
For reuse and flexibility, favour object composition over class inheritance.
Class inheritance is white-box reuse: a subclass is exposed to its parent's implementation details, so inheritance can break the parent's encapsulation and make a class hard to change in isolation.
Object composition is black-box reuse: collaborating objects are used only through their interfaces, so no internal details are exposed.
Class inheritance is defined statically at compile time, whereas object composition is defined dynamically at run time through references between objects.
Identify the aspect of a design that varies and encapsulate it behind a stable interface, so that changing that aspect does not force changes elsewhere.
An object's class (its implementation) is distinct from its type (its interface): many classes can share one type, and one class can support many types.
Anticipate the likely causes of redesign and decouple the parts of a system most likely to change, because accommodating change after a system is built is costly.

A framework predefines the architecture and design decisions (class partitioning, responsibilities, and thread of control) so that an application designer can concentrate on the application-specific parts.

Acquaintance, in which an object merely knows of another (also called association or the using relationship), is a weaker and more loosely coupled relationship than aggregation, in which one object owns or is responsible for another.
Delegation lets a receiving object forward a request to a delegate object, giving run-time behaviour reuse comparable to inheritance but composable dynamically.
A design pattern is a description of communicating objects and classes customized to solve a general design problem in a particular context.
Design patterns are organized along two dimensions: purpose (creational, structural, or behavioral) and scope (whether the pattern applies primarily to classes or to objects).
Creational patterns abstract the object-instantiation process, making a system independent of how its objects are created, composed, and represented.
Structural patterns concern how classes and objects are composed to form larger structures.
Behavioral patterns concern algorithms and the assignment of responsibilities between objects, describing how objects interact and distribute work.
Class-scope patterns capture relationships fixed by inheritance at compile time, whereas object-scope patterns capture object relationships that can change at run time.
Abstract Factory provides an interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes.
Builder separates the construction of a complex object from its representation, so that the same construction process can create different representations.
Factory Method defines an interface for creating an object but lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate, deferring instantiation to subclasses.
Prototype specifies the kinds of objects to create using a prototypical instance and creates new objects by copying (cloning) that prototype.
Singleton ensures a class has only one instance and provides a global point of access to it.
condition: a class must have exactly one instance reachable from a single, well-known access point

statement: Adapter converts the interface of a class into another interface that clients expect, letting classes with otherwise incompatible interfaces work together.
Bridge decouples an abstraction from its implementation so that the two can vary independently.
Composite composes objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies and lets clients treat individual objects and compositions uniformly.
Decorator attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically, providing a flexible alternative to subclassing for extending functionality.
Facade provides a unified, higher-level interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem, making the subsystem easier to use.
Flyweight uses sharing to support large numbers of fine-grained objects efficiently by separating shared intrinsic state from context-supplied extrinsic state.
condition: an application uses a large number of objects whose storage cost is high and whose state can be split into shared intrinsic and supplied extrinsic parts
exception: objects whose state is inherently context-dependent cannot be shared

statement: Proxy provides a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access to it.
Chain of Responsibility avoids coupling a request's sender to its receiver by giving more than one object a chance to handle the request, passing it along a chain until an object handles it.
Command encapsulates a request as an object, letting you parameterize clients with different requests, queue or log requests, and support undoable operations.
Interpreter, given a language, defines a representation for its grammar together with an interpreter that uses the representation to interpret sentences in the language.
Iterator provides a way to access the elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing its underlying representation.
Mediator defines an object that encapsulates how a set of objects interact, promoting loose coupling by keeping the objects from referring to one another explicitly.
Memento captures and externalizes an object's internal state, without violating encapsulation, so the object can be restored to that state later.
Observer defines a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified and updated automatically.
State lets an object alter its behavior when its internal state changes, so that the object appears to change its class.
