Strategy defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable, letting the algorithm vary independently from the clients that use it.
Template Method defines the skeleton of an algorithm in an operation and defers some steps to subclasses, letting subclasses redefine those steps without changing the algorithm's structure.
Visitor represents an operation to be performed on the elements of an object structure and lets you define a new operation without changing the classes of the elements on which it operates.
The Strategy pattern offers an alternative to conditional statements for selecting behavior: moving the conditional branches into separate Strategy classes removes them from the context.
Introducing a separate object for each state (State pattern) makes state transitions explicit, instead of leaving them implicit in scattered assignments to internal variables.
State and Strategy objects can often be implemented as flyweights and are frequently Singletons.
condition: the state or strategy object carries no intrinsic, per-context state

statement: A concrete factory in the Abstract Factory pattern is often implemented as a Singleton, since typically only one instance per product family is needed.
A Facade object is often a Singleton, because usually only one facade per subsystem is required.
Abstract Factory makes exchanging entire product families easy but makes supporting new kinds of products difficult, because its interface fixes the set of products that can be created.
Abstract Factory is usually implemented with Factory Methods, but it can also be implemented using Prototype.
A decorator changes an object's skin (its responsibilities) while a strategy changes its guts (its algorithm); they are two alternative ways of changing an object.

A decorator and a proxy both forward requests to a wrapped object, but a decorator adds responsibilities whereas a proxy controls access; their differing intent, not their implementation, distinguishes them.
A decorator enhances an object without changing its interface, whereas an adapter gives an object a different interface, which makes a decorator more transparent to clients than an adapter.
In the Memento pattern the caretaker holds mementos but must never operate on or examine their contents, preserving the originator's encapsulation.
A memento can expose a wide interface to its originator and a narrow interface to all other objects; only the narrow interface should be public, to protect the encapsulated state.
Visitor's Accept is a double-dispatch operation: the action performed depends on both the type of the element and the type of the visitor.
Visitor makes adding new operations over an object structure easy but makes adding new ConcreteElement classes hard, because each new element type requires updating every visitor.

Composite makes adding new kinds of components easy and keeps clients simple, but it can make a design overly general, since restricting a composite to particular components then requires run-time checks instead of the type system.
A Composite is often the kind of object that a Builder builds.
Mediator centralizes control of how objects interact, which can make the mediator itself a monolith that is hard to maintain.

Iterator supports both external (active) iterators, controlled by the client, and internal (passive) iterators, which control the iteration themselves; active and passive describe the client's role, not the iterator's level of activity.
A template method should call clearly identified primitive (hook) operations, and a naming convention such as a Do- prefix marks the operations that subclasses are meant to override.
Design patterns serve as targets for refactoring: knowing the patterns helps you recognize where a design should head and refactor toward it.

A concrete class is a class with no abstract operations and so can be instantiated, whereas an abstract class declares operations it does not necessarily implement and is not meant to be instantiated directly.
A subsystem is an independent group of classes that collaborate to fulfill a set of responsibilities.
